items.body: Listening to “adventurous” music can be a hazardous activity. It often prompts a familiar question from unsuspecting visitors: “What is this noise?” toppe bianche 白色补丁 by Li Song / Luciano Maggiore begins precisely at that point of uncertainty, asking not only how one should listen to a work, but whether listening can ever be separated from the circumstances in which it takes place. Recorded beneath the railway arches and across the marshes of Walthamstow, London, the album functions as a negotiation between portable electronics, passing trains, weather, wildlife, and human activity. Consisting of two long-form mirror pieces, “/ * /” and “* / *“, the album is built around simple materials: glissandi, friction-like textures, environmental sounds, and interludes of white noise. The title, which translates as “White Patches”, refers to the masking processes used in post-production and the way the different sounds are connected. Trains become white noise, while birdsong, distant conversations, footsteps and accidental events drift in and out of focus. As the artists themselves insist, there is no background here. Everything is present all the time. What soon becomes apparent is the way toppe bianche 白色补丁 refuses to privilege any single element. The portable speakers generating the glissandi are no more important than the arch itself, the trains overhead, or the occasional passer-by. The music exists in a state between composition and improvisation, intention and accident. The sounds feel fragile, yet stubbornly present. They neither demand attention nor disappear entirely. For those not having a tape deck, headphones might reveal the intricate layering of the recording. Personally, I feel the album especially rewarding when played through my laptop speakers in an ordinary domestic environment especially on hot summer days. With windows open, street noise, birds outside, distant traffic, even the hum of household appliances become inadvertent extensions of the piece. In this sense, Toppe Bianche is not simply a recording but a framework for listening. Like the cliché of the tree falling in the forest, it raises questions about perception and presence. The glissandi may occasionally vanish beneath trains, white noise or the sounds of one’s own surroundings, but they continue to exist. That quiet insistence may be the album’s most radical gesture. In the following interview conducted by email Li Song and Luciano Maggiore elaborate on the production process. Li Song and Luciano Maggiore This recording was made beneath the railway arches and across the marshes of Walthamstow, with passing trains becoming an integral part of the sound world. Rather than attempting to isolate yourselves from the environment, you chose to add white noise and work with it. How did the location shape the music, and at what point did the surrounding sounds cease to be “background” and become collaborators in the piece? Luciano Maggiore: The simple fact that we chose to use that arch in the marshes says a lot about how much we wanted the recording to be entangled with the place. It’s a place we both know quite well, having been the location of a small, almost spontaneous festival of experimental music organised by a few friends and us some years ago. The main characters in the work are, of course, the sounds produced by us during the acts of recording and post-production, but the flesh of the pieces, and the world they inhabit, is that arch itself, with its inhabitants and all the accidents imposed by the surrounding sonic life. There is no background. Everything is present all the time. Li Song: Both Luciano and I are quite familiar with the space itself. A couple of years back, the two of us and some friends did an outdoor show under the exact same arch. We both live near the marshes but in opposite directions, so I wouldn’t be surprised if the arch is actually the midpoint between our homes in London. When we decided to record outdoors, that was the first space that came to mind. I think the location sort of designed the piece, in a way we didn’t expect it to at the start. We had chatted about the idea of masking very early on, which is putting one audio signal on top of another to cover it up. But then we sort of forgot about it and went down the route of recording glissandos under the arch. Later on, while working with the recordings, the idea came back to us. The white noise masking, around and over with the train, holds the pieces together. The album is described as existing between composition and improvisation, and between human dialogue and environmental processes. Can you talk about how decisions were made during the recording? Were there agreed structures, or did the piece emerge through listening and reacting to each other, the trains, and the acoustics of the space? LM: The pieces had a backbone that was decided a priori: the use of glissandos, a series of movements through the space, and a range of frequencies we could work with in both pieces. Decisions were then made in situ, following recording attempts and small trials and errors, to understand whether the choices made beforehand suited the situation we found ourselves in. I would say the core idea was to use digital glissandos and, later, fields of white noise to mask certain parts of the recordings. Li Song built a simple piece of software that was easy to control, with an array of parameters (frequency and duration, if I remember correctly). We performed with the software using our phones, each connected to an identical Bluetooth speaker. LS: If I remember correctly, we only had the moving glissando idea and the location planned out. We left pretty much everything else to the day of the recording. Both of us are quite flexible and just open to seeing what happens. I had programmed an oscillator app on a webpage so we could use our portable speakers to generate the glissando sounds. That’s the continuous sound you hear in the recordings, where you can change the pitch range and certain timing settings. On the day, I showed Luciano how to use it, and we briefly talked about how we would move around the space. We did maybe two or three sessions with different settings and configurations. I feel like as we recorded the latter half, we started improvising more and ignoring the rules we had set at the beginning. After that, we just went home to listen back and work on it later. It was during that later process that we had the masking idea with white noise to go along with the train sounds. It didn’t take us long to find an alternative way to mask the other track, and I think the two tracks work better together. Li, your work with No Performance often seeks to minimise the presence of the performer, while Luciano’s practice frequently examines performance itself, repetition, endurance and the theatricality of sound production. How did these seemingly different approaches interact during this collaboration? Did either of you find yourselves working outside your usual habits? LM: Even though our approaches may appear different, both of us perform in various formations that use performativity as a way of staging situations involving sound. Li Song often performs with the artist Mengting Zhuo, and both of us are part of a trio with On Yee Lo, among other collaborations. I would say that neither of us felt in any way out of place LS: The ‘No Performance’ idea actually started out as a series of experiments that Zhu Wenbo and I were doing in Beijing back in 2015. We were doing pieces where the computer listened to acoustic instruments and did its own thing according to the program we had designed beforehand. It was maybe a half-joke to name it ‘No Performance’ because I would just start the program and sit there doing nothing. To be honest, we eventually explored other ideas beyond this style. So it’s not some strict rule I follow throughout all my music. Having said that, I do feel I have grown more attached to the idea of letting things perform by ‘themselves.’ I do believe that somehow shows in this music too. Maybe you could say the different approaches work in different dimensions. I think our approaches overlap more than what it looks like. The liner notes mention a desire to create a music that “eschews self-awareness in favour of a supernatural imbalance.” That is a striking phrase. What does “supernatural imbalance” mean to you in this context? Is it connected to unpredictability, to the agency of the environment, or to a more philosophical idea of dissolving control? LM: That’s a beautiful way of describing the work, but we can’t really claim ownership of the phrase. I think I understand what Cai and Yizhuo (the owners of Aloe) are implying with it, but I would rather leave any explanation to them. LS: To me, my first impression when hearing the track after we add the studio material was actually a sense of balance. Just like the album title, the patch holds things together. Listening to the album, there are moments where it becomes difficult to distinguish between performer, device, environmental sound and recording artefact. Both of your practices seem interested in questioning authorship and intentionality. Do you see this blurring of boundaries as a political gesture, an aesthetic one, or simply the most honest way of engaging with sound today? LM: I’m not sure about honesty. I don’t personally think of what I do as particularly political. There are, of course, other, more effective ways of making a statement than using music to do so. I’m conscious that every position I take in this world carries political value and therefore implies a certain stance. However, I am concerned with music making and the ways in which it can be staged. I believe in making music for music’s sake. LS: I think this is just naturally how we work. With computer or electronic music, there’s a huge appreciation for high-fidelity audio and how many channels you have in your system. For me, ever since my time in Beijing, I’ve performed with my laptop in people’s living rooms, playing through a bunch of cheap small speakers I found for 30 RMB each on Taobao. Not everyone has access to a 16-channel speaker system, and more importantly, there’s just music for laptop speakers. Luciano and I also worked together on the ‘unspecified unspecified unspecified’ concert series in London for a year after COVID. We had this rule of self-amplification, where performers were solely responsible for amplifying their own sound if they needed to. I suppose that’s also related to this idea: people working with their own things, in the space they are given. What is the significance of the title toppe bianche 白色补丁? LM: The Italian toppe bianche can be roughly translated into English as “white patches”. I believe that 白色补丁 is read and understood in more or less the same way. LS: I already referred to title holding things in the above answers, it matches what we were doing with the studio material in the end. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: Adepta Editions have found a kindred spirit in Daniel Pringle. The label’s pursuit of emotive electronics with contortionist rhythms is part of The Jaffa Kid’s DNA. A superb pairing of pieces, two that can ignite the right floor as well as giving the mind space to roam. A bittersweet quality inflecting the contrasting textures For a number of years now, Spain has established itself as a focal point of electronics. Labels like Analogical Force in Madrid, Withhold and Evel in Barcelona, have been flying the flag for thought-provoking machine music that bites with broken beats and undulates with acid. Since 2021, Adepta Editions is a Barcelona based imprint that has taken up the banner of forward thinking electronics. Vinyl has been the medium of choice. Artists like Global Goon, Roger Van Lunteren and ScanOne have graced its doors with a limited pressing run allowing for scope and variety. A new kid is joining the roster, a prolific talent from the British Isles: The Jaffa Kid. No stranger to the above-mentioned labels, The Jaffa Kid (Daniel Pringle) is a dynamo of musical productivity. Dare to look at his Discogs page and you will be gob smacked by the volume of music this man has made. His output is matched by his ability and range. From deep ambient and fragile funk to full-throated jungle and techno, the Newcastle man’s music is a true treasure trove of delights. In Adepta Editions fashion, two tracks make up AE-16. Donning his Qeta pseudonym, Pringle remixes his own work with “Xphor.” The Blitz Mix releases a volley of percussion. Snares surge and rim-shots roll as a tempered tone circles to soulful string. Amen breaks dawn and fade, vocal samples tremble into this churning creation of acute angles and enveloping warmth. Remaining under his Qeta mask, the Blow Mix of “Trigon” races out of the stocks. Despite the piercing percussion speed, a brake is applied to the tempo by the docile and somnambulistic melody. This whimsical fairytale-like key pattern plods through the skittering beats and robust kick, a bittersweet quality inflecting the contrasting textures. Adepta Editions have found a kindred spirit in Daniel Pringle. The label’s pursuit of emotive electronics with contortionist rhythms is part of The Jaffa Kid’s DNA. A superb pairing of pieces, two that can ignite the right floor as well as giving the mind space to roam. AE-16 is available on Adepta Editions. [Bandcamp] AE-16 by The Jaffa Kid  The post The Jaffa Kid :: AE-16 (Adepta Editions) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: The first Wandelweiser release by composer Paul Beaudoin, bright shining light, is now available as a digital album download at Bandcamp. Consisting of the composer’s complete organ works to 2025, the five tracks on this album are performed by Carson Cooman, organist at Memorial Church, Harvard University. Paul Beaudoin is a composer, educator and interdisciplinary artist, born in Hialeah, Florida. He studied at the New England Conservatory of Music and received a PhD in Music Theory from Brandeis University. His music has been performed by the Lydian String Quartet, the Buffalo Quartet and as part of the Piano Spheres series in Los Angeles. In 2015 Paul was awarded a Fulbright Scholarship that brought him to Estonia where he continues to compose and write.Paul Beaudoin writes about bright shining light: “This is not a typical organ recital album. The music moves between fragile resonance, sustained intensity, harmonic pressure, brightness, stillness, and force.” bright shining light is an hour of inspiring organ music that employs all the power of that instrument to draw the listener into a state of contemplation and reflection. The title track of the album opens with a deep, full chord that builds upwards from the lowest registers of the pipe organ. This is a powerful, weighty sound much like the initial sensation of seeing a bright shining light. The notes are all sustained tones, with no perceptible rhythm or beat. The tones in the chord are changing pitch at what seems a glacial pace, but the sound is never static. The chord crowds itself together, suggesting the image of a great cathedral nave reaching ever upwards. As the piece proceeds, higher tones are heard above the bass register, thinning out the sound. The overall feeling becomes more reserved and somber as the piece winds down to its conclusion. The liner notes state that “bright shining light was composed in memory of Alexei Navalny and all those who fight oppression.” There is a definite sense of quiet strength and unyielding resistance here, aided by the perceptive playing of Carson Cooman. The power and intensity of the pipe organ is fully exploited, even without the presence of keyboard pyrotechnics. bright shining light presents a rewarding sonic experience that is both artistically inspiring and resolutely defiant in its realization.et caecitas eorum lacrimas eis efficiet, the second track, translates as “and their blindness shall make them weep.” The composer writes that the piece “…captures the tension between certainty and doubt, inviting listeners to consider the impact of their convictions.” This track continues to exploit the full resources of the organ, opening with a bold, sustained tone in the middle register that is soon joined by more notes to form a chord of intensity and power. These pitches are sustained and vary only slightly once established. At 1:00, a bass pedal tone is added, providing a solid foundation. The texture of the chords thin and thicken as the piece proceeds, reflecting certainty replaced by doubt. At times, the feeling is majestic but without the need for overwhelming the listener with raw power. A high flute tone quietly hangs in the air at the finish accompanied by a soft bass tone that provides a soft landing for this impressive piece. The longest track of the album, at over 23 minutes, is notes of union and longing. This opens with a very low sustained tone, soon joined by a new notes in the middle register. More notes follow to form a lovely chord whose pitches slowly change to create a series of warm and welcoming colors. The tempo is unhurried and the tones are without beat or pulse. At 2:40 some dissonance creeps in as the texture above thins and the low tone in the bass drops out adding an anxious feel. After a short pause, a new chord is formed in the middle to upper registers. The addition of a strong bass tone adds a warm foundation that suggests union after longing. These feelings of separation and union flow in and out as the dissonance in the chords come and go. The chord textures change with and without the bass, while the higher registers dominate to yield a variety of emotional colors. The coming and going of the strong bass tone always decisively shifts the mood to one of warmth and welcoming. When slightly dissonant, the tones in the higher register effectively suggest alienation and longing. Paul Beaudoin writes that “In this piece, my intention was to convey the emotions of union and longing through a delicate interplay of voice-leading and harmony, creating a space for introspection.” The tempo throughout the piece is always slow and deliberate, producing a sense of dignity and gravitas. A very high sustained tone at 14:45 suggests completion, even as the other notes in the chord are searching for resolution. A sense of the familiar is heard in the transparency and consonance of the upper register chords as the piece glides to a peaceful finish. notes of union and longing is a graceful, contemplative piece that gently invites the listener into quiet reflection.stillness emerging, track 4, is written for organ and fixed electronic media. The liner notes explain that “…the fixed electronic soundfield serves as a sonic canvas, providing a rich and immersive backdrop against which the organist paints with musical phrases.” This opens with a soft, low rumbling followed by higher tones that soon join in. As in the rest of the album, these are dense chords that are comprised of sustained tones that slowly change in pitch. The higher tones are most prominent, but very soft with a hospitable feel. Bass pedal tones continue to rumble below, but are almost inaudible. There is a mystical feeling to all of this. As the piece continues, the dynamics in upper notes seem to be slowly increasing, as if emerging. The electronic sounds and the organ blend seamlessly; it is hard to hear where one leaves off or the other begins. A whoosh of wind and a low, recurring scratching in the bass add to the intrigue. The entire piece is quietly serene and the dynamic contrasts are achieved by smooth variations in the texture. stillness emerging ends as it began – quietly. The final track of the album is grace abounding and this opens with a soft pedal tone in the bass. Airy flute tones are heard above in a simple melody and the feeling is both meditative and comforting. Paul Beaudoin writes that “grace abounding explores the concept of grace not as a static, singular experience but as an ever-present force that reaches beyond us, continually flowing and overflowing.” Accordingly, the pedal tone in the bass weaves in and out of the texture with the melody in the upper registers always in the foreground. A sustained, higher pitch often soars above, brightly underlining the melody. At the finish, a resolving chord is heard in the lower registers. grace abounding artfully portrays a process that is constantly at work in our lives, despite our human failings. bright shining light invokes all the majesty of a large pipe organ but expresses that power in harmonic nuance and textural subtlety, drawing the listener into deep reflection as well as into an emotional reaction. Those who appreciate the grand sounds of the cathedral organ will not be disappointed, but should be prepared to find themselves thinking meditatively about this music as well as experiencing its exhilaration.bright shining light is available for digital download at Bandcamp. The post Paul Beaudoin – bright shining light – Album Review appeared first on Sequenza21.

items.body: Ten years is a long time to leave a dancefloor waiting. Buraka Som Sistema have spent most of that decade apart, and on Friday 7 August they walk back onto a UK stage at South London Miniteca: a free, all-day celebration of the Latin American and Afro-Luso communities of South London, out in the open in Burgess Park. Pulling the Main Stage together from midday are ¡Como No!, the capital’s leading Latin promoter since the 1980s and the outfit behind La Linea. The Lisbon crew spent the late 2000s welding Angolan kuduro to European club music, a sound that reached far past Portugal on tracks like “Sound of Kuduro“, made with M.I.A., “Hangover (BaBaBa)“, and “Kalemba (Wegue Wegue)“. Their 2008 album Black Diamond set the template, and two more followed, Komba in 2011 and Buraka in 2014. Years of touring took them from Caracas to Paris, India and Luanda, filmed across those cities in Off the Beaten Track, with an MTV Europe Music Award picked up along the way. They stepped away in 2016 and scattered into solo work, with Branko steering the Enchufada label and Kalaf turning to writing and cultural work. This summer they regrouped for the label’s twentieth anniversary and released “Puro Mambo”, an Angolan-slang title and their first new music in twelve years, alongside a run of festival dates and the first vinyl pressing of their full catalogue. Blaya, whose voice became part of the group’s identity as it grew, is back out front. Where Buraka bent kuduro, Son Rompe Pera bend cumbia, running their marimbas through punk. The second headliners of the festival, the Gama brothers grew up playing the wooden keys at weddings and quinceañeras in Naucalpan, on the edge of Mexico City, alongside their father Batuco; as teenagers they swapped it for punk, then dragged the marimba back with all that noise attached. After Batuco’s death, an invitation from Chilean cumbia veterans Chico Trujillo in 2017 pulled them back to music, and the cumbia punk they play now tips traditional Mexican and pan-Latin songs into garage, ska and surf. A new album, Marimbazos de Oro, follows in September on Mixto Records, produced by the Black Pumas’ Adrian Quesada, with lead single “Nada Que Hacer”. Live, they pull cumbia dancers and moshers to the same marimba. If Lisbon and Mexico City set the day’s coordinates, the rest of the Main Stage answers from London itself. Pianist Eliane Correa built Las Salseras here as the UK’s first all-female salsa orchestra, ten players drawn from across Latin America and the UK. Cuban percussionists Madelin Espinosa and Lidia María Madruga anchor the rhythm section with Argentine multi-percussionist Gala Celia, and Afro-Latin singer Juanita Euka takes the front, a voice that has carried this music at the Barbican and Glastonbury. Between them they have backed Los Van Van’s Mayito Rivera and Jimmy Bosch and tour with Hans Zimmer and Jessie Ware. Correa, who counts herself as much Argentinian and European as Cuban, is blunt about the all-women line-up, “We are not tokens”, a counterweight to the male bands salsa has run on for most of its life. They mark Celia Cruz’s centenary with “La Vida es un Carnaval” and “Quimbara”, alongside Tito Puente’s “Oye Cómo Va” and deeper cuts from the Queen of Salsa’s catalogue. Latinas of London brings a second all-women line-up to the stage, with Allexa Nava crossing over from the salsa orchestra. Desta French runs it on one rule, Latinas backing Latinas, no one above anyone else. A Camden singer of Colombian and Italian parentage, she was the first UK Latin artist played on BBC Radio with an all-Spanish-language song, back in 2020; she writes across jazz, hip-hop and cumbia, and her nights at the Jazz Café have turned into full-room Selena singalongs. Alongside Nava she brings Xativa, whose folk-leaning songs draw on Spanish and Ecuadorian roots. A second stage, Bailoteo, is given over to Latin American sound system culture, run by Bushbby, who started the Candelita night with Desta French. London-born with Colombian roots, she plays cumbia, champeta, reggaetón and dembow off the systems she grew up around. DJ Sueño joins her with the cumbiatón he sharpened in Rosa Pistola’s Mexico City circle, Sabor a Mi runs from guaguancó through cumbia to afro-house on vinyl, and Movimientos resident Amancai, who grew up in Cartagena, threads Colombian Caribbean sounds through afrobeats. Between sets there are children’s sports, yoga and stretching sessions, DJ workshops and food from across the Latin and Lusophone world, open to every age.   South London Miniteca runs from 12pm at Burgess Park on 07/08 Entry is free, though tickets should be booked ahead. Full details and booking are on Dice   https://rhythmpassport.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/AQN_OqLUuwDQPUykEz7IUF2r_or88TQL8tbWQhzbPiELPxiEZiU8w35P2el5YbcOlFqi1_i3NMCPm9nlnYpo5A10H8oyG-kr4Jq8Pl4.mp4 The post Event Preview: South London Miniteca @ Burgess Park (London; Friday, 7th August 2026) appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.excerpt: Nilsa named “Sofala” after the province in central Mozambique where she grew up, and the song reaches back to her childhood there, at her grandmother’s place in the countryside with no television and no telephone, days given over to dancing and singing. items.body: Nilsa named “Sofala” after the province in central Mozambique where she grew up, and the song reaches back to her childhood there, at her grandmother’s place in the countryside with no television and no telephone, days given over to dancing and singing. It rides on Utsi, a traditional dance from Sofala that lives on the drums. Batuque hand-drummers Abel Isaquiel Maria, Argentino António and Wilson Raposo Vasco carry the rhythm, with Michi Wipf on the kit and Gil Mário Nordez on percussion, while Rolf Mosele‘s guitar and André Buser‘s bass weave through, and Dzua Mosele answers Nilsa’s lead in call and response, the Portuguese slipping into Sena, the language of Beira. Nilsa sings herself back into her home region. She names where she is from, Sofala, straight out of Beira, then carries the song west to Búzi, calling people to come with her and meet her sister Laurinda. From there it turns to Dominga de Nhaminga. People call her trouble because she will not stay quiet, standing up to demand her rights, stamping her feet and speaking with her hands until her voice carries all the way to the town of Tica. Nilsa returns again and again to one line: “você não só fala, você faz“, you don’t just talk, you do. Born in Beira, the port city that is Sofala’s capital, Nilsa was one of eight children who built their own instruments and played together. She took her first singing prize at 14, and at 16 joined Djovana, a hip-hop group set up in Beira by two Swiss musicians, which carried her to Switzerland, Germany and South Africa and earned her the name Queen of Mozambican hip-hop back home. She settled in Switzerland in 2001, studied jazz in Bern, and has spent the years since drawing her Mozambican roots through jazz and pop across four albums, from Mamã to Salada Moçambicana. “Sofala” comes now beside a second single, “Emilia”, both of them turning back toward where she began. items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — 'Breathless' is Camel's sixth album and the band's last one with original keyboard player PeterBardens as well as their second and final release to feature Richard Sinclair of Caravan. Thisrecord is a logical continuation of the stylistic evolution of the band's previous albums (startingwith 'Moonmadness' and going through 'Rain Dances'), with Camel exploring a rather accessiblevariation of their melodic style of progressive rock. Scant jazzy interludes can still be heard onthis album, although Mel Collins' presence and impact are virtually non-existent. 'Breathless' mightvery well be classified as an art pop record with proggy arrangements, on which the vocals are asunimpressive as usual.By the way, the vocal duties on this album are divided equally between R. Sinclair, who isundeniably the more capable singer, and Andy Latimer, whose limited range works well within thecontext of Camel's mellow (and at times soporific) music. Some of the better songs featured on thisalbum include the title track, which is a sappy art pop number, the much more sophisticated 'Echoes'with its ornate instrumentals and sheltering melodies as well as the 7-minute track 'The Sleeper', asong exhibiting a fancy Canetrbury-esque nuance in the keyboards. 'Summer Lightning' surprises as anice example of danceable prog, while the rest is tame and dreamy, and perhaps not everybody's cupof tea. The album as a whole is decent and enjoyable, but parts of it are truly boring andunremarkable.

items.body: Review by alainPP — SYRINX CALL operates outside of time, with flutes galore exuding a strong folk vibe; Mirrorneuron is an empathy-dispensing AI controlled by Mara?an intricate psychotherapist figure in this supernatural fable that echoes the style of SINGLE CELLED ORGANISM.'Returning' kicks off with a SINGLE CELLED ORGANISM feel?fitting, given the flute that defines the band's signature atmosphere. It's modern progressive rock?layered and ethereal?flowing into'Boundless Choices,' where Kate Bush and Pink Floyd hover in the background alongside warm vocals; a blend of prog and neo-classical styles featuring swirling guitars and an enchanting flute.'Organic Embodiment' carries hints of ANGE in its melody, while Hannes's heavy build-up evokes ELOY. Jens's velvety vocals briefly recall the soaring heights of SYLVAN or classic-era MARILLION. The whole track is sprinkled with flute and female vocalizations.'Are You My Image' features female vocals and an ambient folk-pop sound reminiscent of ENYA or IONA?truly magical; the guitar arpeggios and flute create a moment of simple, ineffable beauty.'Wheels of Emotion' follows, with narration set against the flute, leading to an emotional breakdown featuring a guitar solo that appears out of nowhere?a solemn moment touching greatness, with sharp guitar work reminiscent of MARILLION. The flute-driven folk drift shares this medieval-troubadour-style track with a big 80s-style keyboard solo and a dash of *Different Light*-era vibes.'Yearning' continues the conceptual journey, with the AI ​​narrating the atmospheric space setting. It is a long, building track?saccharine-sweet in its vocals, yet solid and substantial in its instrumentation. The finale, featuring Isgaard's spellbinding vocals, is truly outstanding. "Attachment," featuring Doris, offers a pastoral ballad reminiscent of days gone by?think JADIS or ELOY?showcasing languid six-string work that flirts with a Floydian atmosphere. The keyboards strongly evoke ELOY?delivering that weighty sound perfect for navigating the landscape of German progressive rock?followed by another Floydian outro featuring waves of sound."Emptiness" follows, led by the alto flute for a gentle, melancholic interlude; Isgaard once again takes center stage with an elven vocal performance over a crystalline piano finale."Mind Over Matter" comes next, blending flute and piano into another melting folk-prog excursion, with Jens's keyboard touches guiding the listener toward a heroic fantasy realm; it is an ethereal ballad that eventually crashes into..."Here..." an interlude defined by its dark alto flute?a moment of suspended anticipation."...And Now" brings back the energy with a soft-heavy riff and reverb-laden guitar, recalling the New Age sounds of APSARAS. The melody begins to circle back on itself slightly, though one must acknowledge that sustaining an hour of such high quality is no small feat. It is time to leave; cinematic footsteps sound before Isgaard calls us to..."The Difference," a track redolent of Kate Bush; the epilogue to a musical odyssey, complete with laughter, tears, doubt, and hope.SYRINX CALL has released a musical gem that builds upon the foundation of their previous album. It is a slow musical journey where the tracks weave a spell, causing you to lose yourself and fall under their hypnotic influence. The sound is an energetic and glamorous blend of folk, rock, and prog?sharp, effective, and polished. (4.75)

items.album: Kilmarth interview: the light inside Pierre Soulages’ black on ‘Au bord des Ténèbres…’

items.body: Belgian electronic solo project Kilmarth talks to Side-Line about his new album “Au bord des Ténèbres…”, built around the “Outrenoir” concept of French painter Pierre Soulages, who died in October 2022 at the age of 102. Composer, producer and French teacher Cédric Wattergniaux discusses the album’s link to the recent single “Avant de céder…”, the personal losses that shaped its final stretch, its shift toward French-language track titles, with a vinyl edition via elasticStage. Wattergniaux founded Kilmarth in 2007, taking the project’s name from the Cornish house at the centre of Daphne du Maurier’s novel “The House on the Strand”. After years of writing on the side of his work as a French teacher, he debuted the project in 2018 with the CD mini-album “Catharsis”, a record he has described as growing out of a period of depression, and has since moved through minimal-electro, post-industrial ambient and IDM territory across a steady run of EPs, singles and albums. Au bord des Ténèbres… by Kilmarth Kilmarth interview SL: “Au bord des Ténèbres…” is built on the idea of Pierre Soulages’s “Outrenoir”, black as a surface from which light returns. Soulages died in October 2022 at the age of 102. When did his black paintings first stop you in your tracks, and what happened in that encounter for it to become, years later, an album? Cédric: I think my encounter with Pierre Soulages’s work is relatively recent, about ten years ago. Before that, monochrome did not attract me at all. I found it too simplistic, but that simplicity came mostly from my own relationship to that artistic movement, which I had never taken the time to understand. I looked at those works from afar, without really confronting them. Then I saw several documentaries about Soulages, and something opened. I began to perceive what he was doing, and especially what he was seeking. Soulages is a rebel in the world of monochrome. He is a monochromist, but his approach is at the same time anti-monochrome. He transforms monochrome into a perceptual experience. In his work, black is never uniform. It is sculpted, striated, polished, matte, shiny, carved, smooth, rough. Light clings to it, settles on it, reflects off it, breaks against it. This interplay between material and light spoke to me immediately. I think darkness appeared very early in my life, at the age of seven, with the death of my grandfather. I saw part of my family collapse under the weight of that loss. I remember going to see him at the morgue. It was a horrible sight for me. I still see it now. He had fallen from his truck – he was a driver – and his face was damaged, marked by the mask of death. It forged a kind of darkness in my thoughts, despite myself, I have to admit. That early experience probably prepared the ground for Soulages’s Outrenoir to resonate so strongly in me. I like to place this idea within the concept of human life. Total darkness may not exist. There is always a light within the dark, and it becomes even more perceptible in those moments. It is not the color that creates it, but the relief, the texture, the way the surface welcomes or repels the light. This vision marked me deeply and nourished my way of composing. Soulages is a unique case in the history of contemporary painting, and it is precisely that singularity that stopped me in my tracks and, years later, found an echo in my music. SL: The album text describes darkness as “a living substance where light transforms, withdraws, fractures, and returns in new forms.” A painter can physically place light into the grooves of black paint. You had to do it with sound. How do you make “light in the dark” audible? Which sounds, textures, or production choices carried that role in the album? Cédric: I think I tried to build a layer of background sound that would be dark, driven by a very present bass, sometimes even too present, but intentionally so. That bass is the dark mass, the foundation. On top of it, I added effects and sharper, almost abrasive sounds that scratch at the bass and create tension inside the sonic material. Then come the luminous moments, the more melodic passages. They are the bright relief, the parts that attract the light. They emerge from the dark mass like sparks, openings, breaths. If you listen closely, you can hear it in tracks like “Ce qui vient…”, “Occultation”, or even “Outrenoir”. In each of these pieces, the light is never given; it appears because the texture calls it. SL: The eight tracks follow the stages of an inner journey: emergence, struggle, essence, instability, withdrawal, and finally “Outrenoir” itself. Was this trajectory already there before the first note, or did the story reveal itself as you composed? And did you write the tracks in the order we hear them? Cédric: I composed this album quite quickly, to be honest. At first, it was only meant to be an EP. I thought I would stop there, but I kept writing, and the album started taking shape almost in spite of me. Once all the tracks were finished, I looked for the structure. I listened to it an uncountable number of times to give it a coherent narrative, to understand how each piece could speak to the others. I removed tracks, added some at the last minute, moved sections around, rebalanced atmospheres. I love that stage of creation. It is the moment when the album stops being a series of compositions and becomes a story, an inner path. That is when everything starts breathing together. SL: The album carries a conviction that goes beyond an art history concept: “a life does not disappear when it ends” and “evoking the dead is letting them live again.” This feels lived, not studied. Is there a personal loss behind this album, and if so, what place does that person hold in these eight tracks? Share only what you want to share. Cédric: During the final stages of the album, I lost the mother of my lifelong companion, Valérie. Marianne was an extraordinary woman, complex, cultured, intelligent. My relationship with her was not always smooth, but I had immense respect for her, for the way she lived her life despite the terrible obstacles she faced. Her passing left a huge void. I also lost my father just before that. These two losses, so close together, deeply influenced the way I listened to and finalized the album. I try to find, in the memories I have of them, a way to keep them present in our lives. Their absence is the dark foundation, and the memories, often very joyful, are the light that remains, the light that recalls the happiness of having known them. Their lives continue to resonate, in me and among the people who knew them. Every day, I try to draw inspiration from them. Their strength, their fragilities, their gestures, their values. These traces continue to live in me, and I believe they slipped into the music. The album speaks of a darkness that is never total, of a light that returns despite everything. And that light, for me, is them. SL: In 2018 you told Side-Line that “Catharsis” was born from a depression, that you barely left your studio for six months, and that music had become a form of therapy. Eight years later, you make an album about what remains of a life after it ends. Between these two records, has the role music plays in your own life changed? And what did the people closest to you, the family and friends you thanked at the time, say when they heard this one for the first time? Cédric: I think “Catharsis” really had to be that concept album reflecting my state of mind at the time. Unsurprisingly, I was diagnosed with hypersensitivity. It was the key to my entire existence. One day, in a very naive way, I asked my psychiatrist how long it would take before I was cured. She simply told me that it would never happen. It was unsettling, but also strangely obvious. I was going to have to live with that label, and beyond therapy, there was another path that would become permanent, a true catharsis: musical creation. Music is not something I often share with the people close to me. With some friends, I never talk about it at all. I have a very small handful of friends who are my ears, the ones I let listen to what I compose. For the rest, even in my close family, it is a topic we rarely discuss. I am grateful they are in my life, that they are part of my daily world, but I have to admit that I am not even sure they know they appear in the credits. I am not sure they listen to what I make either. It does not matter. I cannot reach everyone. It is not popular music, and I do not mean that in an elitist way. It is simply music that requires a certain inner disposition, and not everyone wants to or can enter that space. SL: You are a teacher by profession, and the album states that lives continue “in memory, in transmitted gestures, in shared values.” Transmission is literally your job. How much of the teacher is present in this record? Do you think of your students, or of your own teachers, when you write music about what is passed on? Cédric: The relationship between music and my job is quite similar. I never talk about what I compose with my students, and very rarely with my colleagues. Yet I put into practice many things I learned during my studies. I have always loved creating, writing poetry, stories, reviews, comics, children’s tales. I also made mixtapes, drew, painted, took photos, sculpted, worked with wood. Whenever I had the chance, I integrated these practices into my student work, and sometimes even into my classes. When teaching drama, I wrote a few plays, adapted others, worked on staging, scenography, music, projections, integrated videos. It was a period when I was really having fun, when I could gather all my passions in one creative space. In French class, I love working through writing workshops, encouraging students to invent, to discover themselves, to surprise themselves. In history, I enjoy transmitting the values of brilliant figures who shaped our world. Not just their actions, but what they left behind, their ideas, their struggles, their contradictions too. I try to show my students that these figures are not frozen statues, but human beings who tried, sometimes failed, sometimes succeeded, and left traces that still resonate today. It is a way of extending what others transmitted before us, of keeping those values alive in a classroom, in a discussion, in a moment when a student’s perspective opens. I had a few teachers who will stay in a corner of my memory for life, for their talent and especially for the trust they had in my abilities at the time. There were also others who taught me never to do things the way they did. Both inheritances are precious. I love my job deeply, because I never get bored. And above all, I try to make use of all the values people have passed on to me, every hour of every class I teach. It is a way of extending what I received, of letting it live differently. SL: Applying the album’s thesis to the person who created it: when Kilmarth’s music is one day all that remains of Cedric Wattergniaux, what do you hope it will transmit? Cédric: I know I represent absolutely nothing on a human scale, and on a musical scale it is even more microscopic. I do not really know if my music reaches people. I sometimes receive very kind messages, congratulations, I love this, but I remain doubtful. Music mostly helps me express my fears, my turmoil, everything that constantly works inside me. At its core, it is a form of therapy, a selfish process. I make music for myself first, I write lyrics for myself, and I never try to make my tracks more accessible. If it touches some people, of course that would make me happy. Sometimes I feel that certain lyrics could help reflect on mental health issues, to take the time to look at concerns that remain taboo, even if I do not know whether people take the time to read them. I hope a few people might feel a little less alone when discovering them. That would already mean a lot, even if it will probably be fleeting. In a few years, people will probably no longer remember Kilmarth’s music, and that is perfectly fine. SL: The album title and almost all track titles are in French, while previous Kilmarth releases moved between English (“Sociological Veranda”, “My Son of The Moon”), German (“Vergessen”), and French (“Derrière Le Miroir”). Was the choice of French for this album deliberate, and does composing under French titles change anything for you? Cédric: I think the choice of French came naturally when I decided to follow in the footsteps of Pierre Soulages. The choice of a language for a title is never theoretical for me; it simply appears during the composition process. As the track reveals itself, certain words impose themselves, certain sounds become obvious, and this time, French presented itself as the most fitting language. SL: “Sursomption” is the French rendering of Hegel’s Aufhebung, and “Ousia” is the ancient Greek term for essence. Are these philosophical concepts active elements in the album’s story, or markers for the listener? And what does an idea like sublation sound like? Cédric: In this album, the notions of sursomption, which translates Hegel’s idea of Aufhebung, and ousia, which refers to essence in ancient Greek, are not there to tell a story. They are markers that help understand how the music evolves from within, both in the overall listening experience and in the sound of Kilmarth itself. For me, sublation in music feels like a slow transformation where tensions and fragments do not disappear, but are absorbed into a simpler, more essential form. That is exactly what I wanted to do here by stripping Kilmarth’s sound down, refusing endless layers and multiplying ideas, and returning to something minimal where each element exists fully. Ousia then becomes a point of balance, not a theory to remember, but a sonic presence reduced to what remains when all the excess is removed. SL: “Etude sombre et erratique en Cm” sounds like a page from the classical repertoire, key included. You once said you took theory classes at the local academy and tried classical guitar before buying your first synth, a Korg Triton. Is this étude a nod to that training? And what makes it an étude, what were you practicing? Cédric: Sometimes, when I start a track, I pick a key and a style at random, then improvise. The title simply comes from that exercise. To be honest, this very pompous title is mostly a nod to the Dada movement, which I love precisely because it mocked academicism. That bittersweet training gives a solid foundation for understanding music, so you can later shake it up and break free from it. I think it was Picasso who expressed that idea, even if several masters are sometimes associated with the quote. It perfectly sums up the fact that ignoring a rule out of ignorance has no value, while freeing yourself from it through real knowledge allows you to create with authenticity. That said, everything in the naming of this piece is technically accurate. SL: On a lighter note: “Ce qui vient…”, “Avant de céder…”, “Au bord des Ténèbres…” the ellipses are everywhere in your titles. What do those three little dots do? Cédric: This is fantastic, truly. It is the first time I get to talk about this incredible passion for that punctuation mark, so thank you Bernard! Since I was young, I have had a huge fascination for ellipses. My teachers often reproached me for overusing them, but I always felt they had something magical. They extend the reflection, they pass the torch to the reader, they create a suspended space where anything can still happen. They offer a moment to breathe, to leave suspense, to say that the ending is not here yet. For me, it is the most brilliant and enigmatic punctuation mark in the entire grammar. SL: When reviewing the EP “Avant De Céder…”, our critic wrote about “carefully sculpted soundscapes” contrasted with “persistent layers of noise running through the tracks, giving the music a raw, almost archaic quality.” What was your actual working material on the album? Which instruments, sources, and treatments built these tracks? And the third track of that EP reworked an earlier Kilmarth piece: which one, and why did it belong to this project? Cédric: In my previous albums and singles, I worked a lot through layering. I love tracks that reveal a new aspect with each listen. To name only three projects that inspire me humbly, I think of Massive Attack, Front Line Assembly, and Recoil, and more broadly Alan Wilder. I am not comparing myself to these giants, I am far from them, but their way of building sonic layers remains a source of inspiration. This time, to answer your question, I deliberately used fewer instruments and fewer tracks. For drums, I relied on Battery 4 from Native Instruments and products from Audiomodern. For basses, leads, and atmospheres, I worked with Retrologue, the Arturia suite, Kontakt 7, the Korg Monologue, and a few effects. I used fewer samples, more instruments, and some random sources to keep an element of unpredictability. I did not want to exceed twenty tracks in total or multiply layers in my DAW. I also wanted to vary the structure more throughout the piece. As for the new version of “The White Willow”, it is an older track that still means a lot to me, and I wanted to give it a new impulse. SL: “Cherophobia” involved seven guest vocalists and came from your collaboration with Mad Mac. Did you create “Au bord des Ténèbres…” entirely alone, and if so, did the subject require that solitude? Cédric: I really enjoy taking the opposite approach from the previous project. In “Cherophobia”, I gathered many collaborators – voices, artwork, label – explored very different styles, multiplied layers and instruments. For this album, I wanted to do exactly the opposite. I chose to be alone in the composition, aiming for great sobriety, an assumed simplicity, a raw and instrumental music where randomness also has its place. I wanted to handle everything, from artwork to concept, from release to marketing, to regain a form of total freedom. SL: “Cherophobia” was released through Adventurous Music; “Au bord des Ténèbres…” comes out on your own Bandcamp, with a vinyl edition via elasticStage. Why this path, and is this the first time Kilmarth exists on vinyl? What comes next for the project, and is there any chance this material will be played live? Cédric: These are more elements showing that opposite approach. I felt the time had come to create a physical work to humbly get closer to Soulages. I always wanted to release something tangible. I once made a CDR, but I was not really satisfied with it. I also produced cassettes for “Derrière le Miroir”, but when it was time to release them, more personal concerns took over and the tapes stayed in their box. I think they will stay there forever. As for a concert, I do not think I will ever do one. I have a project in mind with videos, scenography, voices, guest instruments, but it would be far too expensive. I do not want to be the person who goes on stage with a laptop, launches their music, and projects a few images. I have nothing against those who do it, if they enjoy it, good for them, but it is not what I want. People who make the effort to come see you must experience something different from what they have in their living room; you must give them something visually and sonically powerful. It has to be a strong moment where you give yourself entirely in creation and energy. I am not financially or materially able to offer something of that scale, so I prefer not to do it at all. Maybe I set the bar too high, maybe it is a mistake, but that is how I feel right now. SL: In 2018 you called music “a legal drug with the immense power to make us escape.” After an album about death, memory, and what remains, does that definition still hold in 2026? And is it still an escape, or has it become something else? Cédric: It is still a parallel world, a way to escape the one we live in. We must admit that the real world does not always offer the positivity human beings need to feel well. There are many ways to get away. I have friends who push themselves through sports, who take on incredible challenges, who devote themselves to sewing, reading, writing, farming, painting, photography, fishing, forest walks. The most important escape for me has always been music, and after all these years, it still is. So many artists have given me so much throughout my life, have made my life more beautiful. I am deeply grateful to them. About Kilmarth Kilmarth is a Belgian electronic solo project founded in 2007 by composer, producer and French teacher Cédric Wattergniaux, mixing IDM, experimental electronics, ambient, cinematic sound design and glitch. The project’s name references Kilmarth, the Cornish house at the centre of Daphne du Maurier’s novel “The House on the Strand”. Wattergniaux studied music theory and classical guitar at his local academy before buying his first synthesizer, a Korg Triton. The project debuted in 2018 with the CD mini-album “Catharsis”, a record Wattergniaux has described as growing out of a depression during which he barely left his studio for six months. Side-Line spoke to him about it that year in the interview “Music Is A Legal Drug That Has The Immense Power To Make Us Escape”. Kilmarth followed with the EP “Derrière Le Miroir” in 2021, pushing into minimal-electro and cinematic territory, and the video-focused single “M-Fia41”. In 2022 came the two-track single “Baryum”, introducing a darker post-industrial ambient angle, followed by the 2023 mini-album “Better Days”, which brought a vocalist into the project for the first time. January 2024 saw Kilmarth’s debut full-length IDM album, “Sociological Veranda”, followed the same year by the single “Vergessen” with its jazz-infused B-side “ToExposeTheTruth”, and the EP “My Son of The Moon”, which introduced Mad Mac as a guest. In early 2025, Kilmarth collaborated with D-Fried on the album “Micrometeoritic Flowerpot”. January 2026 brought the nine-track concept album “Cherophobia” via the Leipzig-based label Adventurous Music, exploring the fear of happiness across seven guest vocal collaborations including Mad Mac, Deranged Psyche, Eeerisei, Silly Shadow, Heri B., Natasha Moreno and Clémence Legrand. In March 2026, Kilmarth released the three-track single “Avant de céder…” as a solo, self-released first glimpse of the next album, later reviewed by Side-Line. That next album is “Au bord des Ténèbres…”, built around Pierre Soulages’ “Outrenoir” concept and shaped in its final stages by the deaths of Wattergniaux’s father and of Marianne, the mother of his partner Valérie. Unlike “Cherophobia”, the new album is written, performed and produced entirely alone, and is planned for release on Kilmarth’s own Bandcamp page with a vinyl edition through elasticStage; a release date has not yet been confirmed.

items.body: Kill Instinct will release their second album, “Kill Two: Behavioral Sink”, on August 7, 2026 through Freak Power. The Toronto electro-industrial duo of Phil Gonzo and Lea Ashley had originally scheduled the digital album for September 18, 2026; the release now arrives six weeks earlier. A Bandcamp listening party precedes it on August 6 at 1:00 AM CEST, where fans can hear the album in full, chat live with the band and ask questions about the record. ‘Kill Two: Behavioral Sink’ tracklist and pre-order The 12-track album carries the tracklist “Unauthorized Disclosure”, “Truth For Silence”, “Fragment Of Reality”, “Ignore The Static”, “Master Or Slave”, “Control”, “People You Love”, “Bury It Deep”, “Found Footage” (featuring Alex Sales), “The Optimist”, “Rat Utopia” and “KI-130”. Several of these tracks already reached listeners as singles ahead of the album, among them “Ignore The Static”, “People You Love”, “Rat Utopia” and “Control”, the latter also released as an Apoptygma Berzerk remix. The digital album is available for pre-order on Bandcamp now. Pre-order buyers receive the already-released singles immediately, with the remaining tracks unlocking on August 7. kill.two//Behavioral Sink by Kill Instinct Across the album, Kill Instinct build on the “behavioral sink” concept and the “Universe 25” experiments first cited when the record was announced in April 2026, tracking themes of surveillance, manipulation and fractured identity against the effects of technology on daily life. About Kill Instinct Kill Instinct is a Toronto electro-industrial duo of Phil Gonzo and Lea Ashley. The project’s debut full-length, the eight-track digital album “Kill.One”, was released on February 27, 2025, with a tracklist including “Funerals”, “Parasocial”, “Grip (Tighter)”, “BIG”, “King of Kings”, “Lovers”, “False Deities” and “Paradise”. A steady run of remixes and standalone tracks followed: “Parasocial (Svjet Zéro Remix)” in May 2025, “Paradise (Vakhtang Remix)” in July 2025, “Funerals (Svjet Zéro Remix)” and “Grip (Tighter) [Forged Reigns Remix]” in August 2025, the standalone single “BIG (VIP)” on November 7, 2025, “BIG (Jalex Remix)” and “Funeral Stripper” in October 2025, “Parasocial (Trakt Null Remix)” in December 2025, and “Funeral Stripper (Night Version)” in January 2026. Outside Kill Instinct, Phil Gonzo has contributed remix work to Matte Blvck’s “Vows”. Kill Instinct began the rollout for “Kill Two: Behavioral Sink” in April 2026 with lead single “Ignore the Static”, followed by “People You Love”, “Control” – which also received the Apoptygma Berzerk remix – “Bury It Deep” and “Rat Utopia”. The album was originally set for September 18, 2026; Kill Instinct have now moved it up to August 7, preceded by an August 6 Bandcamp listening party.

items.body: Talking Heads released their third studio album, “Fear of Music,” on 3 August 1979 through Sire Records. The album turns 47 this year. Produced by Brian Eno and the band, “Fear of Music” followed “More Songs About Buildings and Food” (1978) and preceded “Remain in Light” (1980), the middle record of three consecutive Eno collaborations that reshaped the band’s sound. Talking Heads recorded the album’s basic tracks on 22 April and 6 May 1979 at drummer Chris Frantz and bassist Tina Weymouth’s loft in Long Island City, Queens, using the Record Plant’s mobile studio, then completed the record at the Hit Factory, Atlantic Studios, RPM Studios and Record Plant in New York City. Greg Calbi mastered the album at Sterling Sound. The eleven-track album is sequenced across two sides: “I Zimbra,” “Mind,” “Paper,” “Cities,” “Life During Wartime” and “Memories Can’t Wait” open the record, followed by “Air,” “Heaven,” “Animals,” “Electric Guitar” and “Drugs.” King Crimson guitarist Robert Fripp guests on opener “I Zimbra,” whose lyrics set a Hugo Ball Dada poem to music. “Fear of Music” streams on Spotify. About Talking Heads Talking Heads formed in New York City in 1975. David Byrne and Chris Frantz had played together as the Artistics at the Rhode Island School of Design from 1973, joined by fellow student Tina Weymouth on bass after the trio moved to New York City in 1975. The band played its first show as Talking Heads on 5 June 1975, opening for the Ramones at CBGB. They signed to Sire Records in November 1976 and released their first single, “Love → Building on Fire,” in February 1977. Jerry Harrison, formerly of the Modern Lovers, joined on keyboards and guitar in March 1977, completing the lineup. The debut album “Talking Heads: 77” followed in 1977 and produced the single “Psycho Killer.” “More Songs About Buildings and Food” (1978) marked the band’s first collaboration with Brian Eno and included a cover of Al Green’s “Take Me to the River,” which became the group’s first Billboard Top 30 hit. “Fear of Music” (1979) continued the Eno partnership, mixing post-punk with funk and disco rhythms, and “Remain in Light” (1980) closed the trilogy with West African polyrhythms drawn from Fela Kuti’s music, which Eno had introduced to the band. Talking Heads reached its commercial peak in 1983 with “Speaking in Tongues” and the US Top 10 single “Burning Down the House.” The following tour was filmed by Jonathan Demme for the concert film “Stop Making Sense” (1984). “Little Creatures” (1985) became the band’s best-selling album, “True Stories” (1986) served as the soundtrack to Byrne’s film of the same name, and “Naked” (1988) became the group’s final studio album. Byrne left the band in 1991 and Talking Heads disbanded. The band was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2002, reuniting briefly to perform. The 47th anniversary of “Fear of Music” places the album at the midpoint of Talking Heads’ three-album run with Eno, between “More Songs About Buildings and Food” and “Remain in Light.”

items.body: Alchera Vision has released the Castle Party 2026 compilation, a limited digiCD tied to the annual Castle Party festival at Bolków Castle, Poland. The release is out this week, on 7-8 August 2026. It comes in a 3-panel digipak with 19 tracks running 71 minutes, and is distributed in Europe through Audioglobe. Castle Party 2026 by Various Artists The “Castle Party 2026” compilation continues an annual series that Alchera Vision has produced alongside the festival since at least 2014, pairing festival headliners with newer acts and offering radio edits, remixes, video versions and tracks making their first appearance on CD. The 2026 edition mixes acts who played this year’s Bolków edition with others connected to the festival’s wider circle, spanning EBM, darkwave, gothic rock, post-punk and industrial styles. Castle Party 2026 compilation tracklist Empathy Test – “Monsters” (Radio Edit) – 04:00 Ash Code – “Nostalgia” – 03:13 A Projection – “No Control” – 03:02 Mayflower Madame – “A Foretold Ecstasy” – 04:36 Long Night – “Ghost” – 03:55 The Last Digital Angel – “One” – 02:38 Tribulation – “Drink The Love Of God” – 02:56 Merciful Nuns – “Elysene” – 03:19 Moonspell – “Opium” (Radio Edit) – 02:46 Agonised Too – “Lurking Fear” (Video Version) – 04:11 This Morn’ Omina – “(The) Rûach (of God)” [CCF] – 04:57 Rue Oberkampf – “Eternity” – 04:21 Denuit – “Wounded Heart” (Mila Dietrich Remix) – 03:00 Sierra Veins – “My Poison” – 03:27 Unter Null – “Coming Up To Breathe” – 05:32 Dawn Of Ashes – “Viral Decay” – 04:14 Hocico – “Hey Tú!” (with Prayers) – 04:12 Xotox – “Leben und Sterben für Musik aus Strom” (EXT!ZE Remix) – 03:33 She Pleasures Herself – “Last Goodbye” – 03:42 Several acts on the “Castle Party 2026” compilation played this year’s festival at Bolków, among them Empathy Test, Hocico, Denuit, A Projection, She Pleasures Herself, Long Night, This Morn’ Omina, Agonised Too and Rue Oberkampf. Sierra Veins, who also performed at the 2026 edition, contributes “My Poison” to the tracklist. About Castle Party Castle Party began on 20 August 1994 at Grodziec Castle, drawing around 300 people to see five Polish bands early in their careers: Moonlight, Daimonion, T.R.H., Pornografia and Fading Colours. The festival outgrew Grodziec within a few years and moved to Bolków Castle in 1997, the enclosed medieval courtyard setting it has kept since. Attendance grew from roughly 800 in 1995 to around 4,000 by 1999, when Clan of Xymox headlined. Castle Party became a three-day event in 2000, and its 2026 edition ran across four days, from 16 to 19 July, with a line-up including Moonspell, Diary of Dreams, Hocico, Empathy Test, Rotersand, Covenant and XOTOX across the Castle Stage and Park Stage. Side-Line covered the full 2026 timetable in May and published a four-day report from Bolków after the festival. Held annually at Bolków Castle in Poland, it is described as the biggest festival of its genre in Eastern Europe. About Alchera Vision Alchera Vision is the Polish label behind the annual Castle Party compilation series, releasing new editions to coincide with the festival and distributing them in Europe through Audioglobe. Its back catalogue includes prior “Castle Party” compilations dating back to at least 2014, alongside catalogue numbers such as the TRAITRS debut album “Rites and Ritual”, first released via the label in May 2017. The “Castle Party 2026” compilation extends that yearly series, again drawing its tracklist from artists connected to the festival’s line-up and circle.

items.body: Digital Factor was founded more than 30 years ago, yet the project led by Mike Langer shows no signs of losing momentum. On the contrary, it continues to surprise and evolve. For this new album, Gwendolyn Gaffa officially joins the lineup, contributing to a concept inspired by the creative spirit of 80s New-Wave. It would be unfair to dismiss this as a mere imitation of ’80s music. Instead, Digital Factor revisits the production techniques, instruments, and sonic aesthetics that defined the decade, transforming them into a contemporary and distinctive sound. While many of the tracks subtly reference influential acts from that era, they never come across as derivative. I can hear echoes of Kraftwerk, Depeche Mode, and Fad Gadget, yet these influences are skillfully reinterpreted into an experimental form of Minimal-Electro that remains unmistakably Digital Factor. At first, “0.8” may not reveal all its strengths. It is not an immediately accessible album, but one that gradually draws the listener in and continues to surprise with its rich blend of influences and ideas. There are several outstanding tracks to discover here, making this, in my opinion, one of the strongest albums Digital Factor has ever released. The occasional female vocals add an extra layer of variety and elegance to the overall sound. “0.8” is likely to challenge listeners precisely because it refuses to fit neatly into a single niche. Yet that is also its greatest strength. Rather than reinventing itself completely, Digital Factor embraces innovation by reimagining the legacy of the 80s, resulting in an album that feels both nostalgic and strikingly forward-looking. (Rating:9). The album was preceded by the “They Will Forget You (When You Die)” EP, which served as its first preview. Listen to “Poor Mind”: Poor Mind by Digital Factor About Digital Factor Digital Factor started in Altenburg, Germany, in 1993. Formed by Mike Langer, Torsten Heise, and Tino Schmidt, the later line-up phases included Guido Litke and Leo von Leibnitz. Musically the project brings a mix of EBM and electro with later on also synth-pop, techno, and crossover elements. The first release was the 1994 Hard Records EP “F.A.L.L.I.N.G.-Down”. A move to Hyperium / Hypnobeat followed, bringing “Relationchips” in 1995, “On Demand” in 1996, “De Facto” and “Countercheck” in 1997, and “Over One Million Times” in 1999. After a quieter period, the band returned with “One More Piece” in 2006, “Look Back To Go Forward” in 2009, and “Trialog” in 2011. Alfa Matrix signed the band in 2020 and released “Come With Me”. That release was followed by “A Chemical Process” in 2021, a few back-catalogue reissues, the “What?” EP in 2022, and in 2023 the singles “I Am What I Am” and “Ouvre”, along with the charity album “G.B.A.-General Behavior Abrogate”. Gwendolyn Gaffa joined Mike Langer as a permanent studio and live member ahead of the “They Will Forget You (When You Die)” EP, released in April 2026 as the first preview of “0.8”, the full album reviewed here.

items.body: Band: beauty is the end | Album: White Knuckle Dress | Genre: Art rock, Progressive pop | Bandcamp Ever wonder what Spock’s Beard might sound like if they were a lightly-folky art-pop band? Well, I think beauty is the end is a pretty good approximation of that idea. Their songs are long and complexly-structured, with some flashy and emotive instrumentalism. Tones are mostly bright, but they also ably deploy tense, minor-key moments well. I really enjoy how prominent violin is throughout the record, and melodies are pretty consistently catchy. Certain passages are a bit cheesier than I’d normally go for, but this record is an overall success. The 10-minute “Domesticated” is a definite highlight. Score: 76/100 Band: Brass Camel | Album: Brass Camel | Genre: Progressive rock | Bandcamp Brass Camel’s third album is a peppy, punchy, enthusiastic, and unashamedly retro-sounding record. They lean heavily into classic rock, hard rock, and glam rock tropes and imbue it with Yes-like technical flashiness. They remind me a lot of acts like (early) Kansas or some of Queen’s more ambitious moments. The sound is maximal and bright, and they effortlessly weave catchy pop melodies alongside complex instrumental displays. I wouldn’t call this an essential release, but it’s a lot of fun, and it’s an example of how to do proggy retro-rock well. Score: 75/100 Artist: Me El-Ma | Album: Forward Owner | Genre: Progressive rock | Bandcamp The newest solo album from Israeli drummer and composer Me El-Ma demonstrates a lot of ambition and some stellar performances. The music is complex and diverse, drawing from classic prog, avant-garde influences, folk, classical, and Levantine music. Unfortunately, this can frequently result in a lot of songs coming off as muddled, unfocused, and complicated for complication’s sake. The vocals are also strikingly similar to those of Jon Anderson, and the credit being given to “VIRJA” makes me think they may be artificially-generated. (I’m guessing VIRJA stands for something like Virtual Intelligent Recreation of Jon Anderson.) And I wonder if Jon Anderson gave his okay for his voice to be used like this. (I’m also fairly confident that the guitars are programmed, but I have no real issue with that, as El-Ma says all this was written by him.) Score: 53/100 Band: Korbo | Album: Amnésiste | Genre: Progressive rock | Bandcamp This French quartet plays an energetic, relatively heavy variety of progressive rock. Their sound is impactful and powerful, drawing from classic hard rock, punk, and metal. Occasional jazzy licks serve as nice points of contrast. “Chaînes” sees the band dip into some mild doom and sludge flavors, though parts of this particular cut can feel a bit dragged-out. In general, though, despite the long runtimes, most of the songs feel well-structured. Score: 74/100 Band: Osees | Album: Cara Maluco EP | Genre: Krautrock, Psychedelic rock | Bandcamp Ever-prolific psych-punks Osees are back with a new EP of wiry psychedelia. Elements of punk, post-punk, and noise rock are prominent here. This is Osees at a moment when they’ve shifted their focus back to guitar-based music, in contrast to their frequent synth excursions. The sprawling title track is energetic and fun, if a bit unfocused, and I love the twangy tones of “Joro”. “Synaptic Static” is bright and sunny, but it feels a little underbaked. The closing “Joy in Oblivion” is the weirdest and wildest cut on this release, despite clocking in at under two minutes, and it’s probably my favorite here. Score: 73/100 Band: Tortue | Album: Mëändyou | Genre: Zeuhl, Progressive electronic | Bandcamp This one-man act from St. Louis presents a completely unexpected but deeply enjoyable vision for zeuhl on this album. The album title is taken from The Turtles’ “Happy Together”, vocal samples from which play a prominent role on this album. In addition to Magmatic repetition and jazzy instrumental tones, high-energy electronica (which I think might be classifiable as drum-and-bass; I’m not 100%, as I’m hardly an expert) keeps this sonic experiment zipping along. This 40-minute, four-part suite has moments of both great intensity with maximal arrangements and more restrained passages that often cultivate dread. My one real gripe about Mëändyou is its length. There are a lot of cool ideas, but parts of this record can feel a bit on the needlessly-drawn-out side of things, even by the standards of a repetition-loving genre like zeuhl. Score: 70/100
