items.body:
The momentous Chain Reaction full-length debut by Robert Henke and Gerhard Behles aka Monolake, issued on vinyl for the very first time on its 25th anniversary and still sounding as sleekly futuristic as ever.

Replete in its definitive remastered edition, which features additional field recordings of rain and insects on ‘Cyan’, Monolake’s debut album is a masterclass of late ‘90s techno straddling widescreen ambient soundscapes and pulsing, Berlin-standard dub techno. It gathers tracks from 1996’s preceding 12” releases, ‘Cyan’, ‘Lantau /Macao’, and ‘Occam / Arte’ plus ‘Index’ from his Helical Scan project, in a landmark album that, with hindsight, can be heard as a milestone between early ‘90s ambient techno and subsequent, sleeker forms of minimalism and spatialized sound design that reflected and deeply influenced techno and electronic music to come.

The re-edit of ‘Cyan’, teeming with insectoid nanorhythms and the patter of rain, opens a seminal set that distills the head-long energy of ‘90s techno to a blissful sublime without losing its vital propulsion. In the tunnelling dynamic of ‘Index’ thru the exquisitely light-footed stepper ‘Occam’ he conceives a sort of techno purism comparable with Basic Channel but distinguished by its relatively crisp contours and HD definition. But he also proves equally adept at other routes and branches of techno, as with the slow, heaving designs of ‘Lantau / Macau’, which impressionistically convey his times spent in the Far East through mutated field recordings, while the radiant ‘Arte’ is a masterpiece of downtempo ambient techno, and ‘Mass Transit Railway’ ropes in fellow synth fiend Wieland Samolak, who wrote user manuals and their translations for Emu Systems and Sequential Circuits - for a floating high-water mark of ‘90s ambient ambient sound design.

items.body:
Dean Blunt’s totemic, genre-agnostic first ’Black Metal’ album is back in circulation on the heels of its killer 2nd volume, singing out a singular sort of mid-decade London blooz where his myriad circles run into one.

In 2014 ‘Black Metal’ arrived as Blunt’s 4th solo album in a string of quietly groundbreaking and guess-again solo recordings following the break-up of Hype Williams, his duo with Inga Copeland. It was an instant fave, raved about everywhere, and with the benefit of hindsight is arguably one of the past decade’s definitive highlights; a record symptomatic of the way staid generic borders were dissolving, expressing a lucid but woozy pathos that still feels timeless, yet very much of its flat-time, when the stream of musical history had pooled into the reservoir of the internet.

Returning to its slow baked charms years later ‘Black Metal’ has lost none of its allure, with a reflective stillness still belying its depths. Nimbly joining wipe clean presets and crisp licks of original instrumentation with vocals by Blunt and regular spar Joanne Robertson, their baker’s dozen tunes somehow consolidate aspects of everything from hip hop to chamber music, indie-pop to R&B with experimental wit and ohrwurming magick that places it among his most memorable and surprising records.

From the symphonic Americana lilt of ‘Lush’ to its amazing 13 minute centrepiece of chamber soul gauze ‘Forever’ and the free jazz meets folk and roadrap synthscape of ‘Grade’ it coolly piques curiosity and perplexes from every angle, resolving unfamiliar styles with a pop-sharpened manner that follows a path first taken by A.R. Kane and which quite possibly ignited a reappraisal of the problematic way in which Black music has been perceived and categorised in popular/critical culture.

All time business = unmissable.

items.body:
12th Isle push the boat out to Rosso Polare’s uchronic folklore, pulling from the Milanese artist’s Italian folk heritage and weaving in chops by Persian electro-acoustic artist Cinna Peyghamy, plus Italian avant-garde veteran Riccardo Sinigaglia, for an adventurous session braiding folk and concrète timelines... 

“Cacciamali is an exploration of diegetic sound, folk chants and traditional rhythms and instrumentation building upon Milan based Rosso Polare’s last outing Campo Amaro and the subsequent departure of co-founder Anna Vezzosi from the group. Where the 2024 album incorporated a heavy use of folklore as a new tool, Cacciamali explores the influence further by bringing in a host of collaborative players including Italian avant-garde veteran Riccardo Sinigaglia, sound artist and researcher HMOT (Stas Shärifulla) and Persian/Parisian electro-acoustic musician Cinna Peyghamy.

‘Scoff Back Sickness’, as the title loosely translates, utilises the same approach, one based on non-hierarchical authorship and leaning heavily on field recordings that both contrast and blend with the tonal material, focusing on biophony, landscape and environmental audio as compositional material. Shifting closer now to a shared network of voices and materials, the dual narrative unfolds as such:

Side A is connected to the concept of the medieval quintain games, specifically flag throwing, where certain drumming patterns from the tradition have been overworked, distorted and transformed. Side B is an underlying local legend from the north of Italy, where some sources speak of a presumed duel in 1744 between a father and his son, ultimately ending with the son’s death. These two layers are not illustrative but structural: ritual / repetition / tradition on one side, and rupture / conflict / loss on the other. A struggle to keep floating, a long shout in the distance, suspended between memory, ritual and disappearance. The result is dense, thick with impulse yet also measured, and often leaves us disoriented and questioning a sound's origin the moment we think we have a grip on the process. The gentle nostalgia of close-mic’ed ‘Falò’ summons the spirit of René Aubry & Jean Schwarz’s concréte masterpiece ‘Five Women’ on the Still Waters ballet soundtrack, and the stark contrast of looping rhythms on both ‘Xiv - Pavo’ and ‘Monte’ deploys a driving, intentful break from the moments of worldly human interactions served by the field recordings.”

items.body:
Not the birth of acid house, but a thrilling piece of synth raga set to brisk disco beats, Bollywood soundtrack composer Charanjit Singh’s ’82 LP is simply a landmark in its own right, and a proper ‘floor-filler to boot.

Since its first reissue in 2010, Singh’s cult, early use of the TB-303 on driving machine beats has been erroneously hailed the birth of acid house. OK the formula is there, but Chris Carter’s ‘Spaces Between’ (1980) and his CTI jam ‘Dancing Ghosts’ got there a couple of years before Singh, at the very least, and neither really inform the genius of Phuture and co a few years later. In any event, ‘Synthesizing: Ten Ragas To A Disco Beat’ is just an incredibly fruity boost to any club, revolving 10 hypnotic, pulsating jams closer to early Irdial (say, Aqua Regia’s ‘Hot Love’) than owt from the Chi. 

Taking a minute away from knocking out Bollywood scores and leading his wedding band covering popular songs, Singh would land upon a stroke of genius with ‘Ten Ragas To A Disco Beat’, finding the sweetspot between prevailing hi-NRG disco and millennia of raga traditions that patently transcended the sum of their parts more than 40 years later. It sounds very much of its time, rather than the stripped back linearity of later acid house, evidenced in the florid keyboard urges of ‘Raga Bhupali’, transposing a steamy sort of club canter to somewhere even more humid.

A real club evergreen, suck it and see.

items.body:
2nd wave dub techno staple Stephen Hitchell meets new wave producer Federson in a back ’n forth of timeless originals and versions.

San Francisco’s Chris Kelly, aka Federsen’s Alt Dub label hosts this passing of the baton/torch with CV313 and Echospace figure Hitchell a sits 2nd release after the ‘Positive Charge’ EP  christened the vessel in earlier ’24. Federsen fronts the session with a smoky, night-driving dub of CV313’s ‘Skycrossing’ in properly classic Maurizio style, especially that scooping bassline, whilst shutting it down with the more air-stepping levity of his dusted congas and distant dub chords to ‘Skyway’.

CV313’s original ‘Skycrossing’ places his mastery of constantly shifting, ever the same, dynamic within its unfurling envelopes, alongside a remix of ‘Skyway’ that plunges upward, outward into billowing electro-acoustic dub techno dimensions.

items.body:
On a label full of weirdos, outliers, mavericks and freaks, clandestine Greek anomaly Aeson Zervas is Heat Crimes’ OG wildcard, landing a debut album a couple of years ago that sounded like The Caretaker channeling crates of rebetika, and now returning with this deeply elusive new LP of plasmic synths that unfolds in ways that will leave you with a proper motion sickness of time travel. Aye, it’s a special one.

After lighting up 2024 with blink ’n miss LP & tape drops, Aeson Zervas’s 3rd instalment dips into a perpetual night world of cobwebbed keyboard melodies and flame flicker incantations designed to score your next regression session. As ever, the label and artist remain tight-lipped about pretty much everything, but the vibe is self-evidently clammy and febrile thru a dozen parts familiar to both preceding drops, woven between pillars of inspiration in lemniscate loops and free flowing rhythmelodic arrangements that bind his ideas to bezonked minds.

The Mesolonghi-based enigma continues to prove a master of hypnosis and a conduit for ancient spirits seeping into the modern world, luring susceptible minds to states of bliss and dread, but not without that sense of romance that also lit up his prior releases. Once again feeling the same pull of past worlds as The Caretaker, only slanted to microtonal scales, his mix of lopped-off and extended melodies tell arcane stories still salient to contemporary imaginations able to tune in.

Activating with a section of meditative, almost no-wave strafing discord, themes of shimmering exotica slide into backyard ritualism, with a lilting marimba sounding like it escaped a Martin Denny side before bleeding into a Giallo-esque wheeze, thru port and island-hopping rebetika, and properly haunting passages of midnight sacred music swarmed by cicadas. The 6th (Χωρίς τίτλο 23) part of needling Italianate arps and screeches is particularly affective, as is the plugged-in folkdance sputter of the 8th (Χωρίς τίτλο 25), and a final couplet coming off like Muslimgauze with a thing for sleazy horror, not dub.

Basically, whatever this label serve, lap it up while you can.

items.body:
Lovers of ZudRangMa, Khruangbin, and even the White Lotus 3 soundtrack will be enchanted with Korlakang’s chiming, low-slung meld of ’70s psych pop and Luk Thung from the quieter side of Bangkok...

“Korlakang are four young friends from Thonburi, the quieter, canal-laced western bank of Bangkok, where temple bells and river rhythms shape everyday life. Formed from a bond that stretches back to high school hallways and shared university years, the band came together with a sound rooted in Thai traditional music and the warm haze of psychedelic rock.

Their debut 7-inch, Samong Sai, is that rare thing: a record that seems to arrive already aged, carrying the grain and warmth of a forgotten 70s pressing. It seeps in slowly, sweet and chill, like sound faintly coming through a neighbour's window. The kind of music that makes you stop what you're doing just to hear a little more of.”

items.body:
Dreader than dread dub vapors from Ghost Dubs, in a lineage stretching from Dadawah to Burial Mix, Vainqueur to Resilent, Pole to Rod Modelll...​

Toiling in Berlin’s deep seam of abstract dub practice that scrolls back to Rhythm & Sound’s earliest via Pole’s dusty convections and Chain Reaction's fritzed mutations; Ghost Dubs embodies the art of dub as method with a strong haul of dematerialised, sludgy tramplers operating close to the scuzzy heart of Kevin Martin, aka The Bug. Uncompromisingly in-the-zone and dank as a bong, the dozen cuts get right under the skin, up-the-pharynx, with an intoxicatingly sedated and hallucinatory quality that impresses murky, vaporous patterns on the back of blunted eyelids and may possibly raise knees to its slompy skank and imaginary physics. 

Of course, the sound is rooted in the innovative, half century-old traditions of Jamaican dub, as established by King Tubby and Lee “Scratch” Perry, and developed by the likes of Scientist or Mad Professor. But Ghost Dubs picks it up at the point where it diffused into techno and noise during the ‘90s, taking that sound as a jump-off into his microcosm of granular, atomised atmospheric disintegration that nevertheless holds to a steady ballast of scoop-worrying sub-bass tremors. No doubt anyone who’s followed the devolution of this sound outside Jamaica, from NYC illbient to Berlin dub techno, will recognise his hands-on-desk tekkerz ushering the sound into oblique new spaces with a canny sense of proprioception that locates it somewhere in fissure between classic and contemporary soundspheres.

From the caustic attrition of ‘Chemical’, thru the inverted mulch of ‘Dub Lobotomy’, to the sensuous but elephantine trample of ‘Hot Wired’ and tumescent swell of ‘Circles Lines’ ,Ghost Dubs leaves his clammy fingerprint on every cut. Some are primed to bend your Clarks, as with the bilgy step of ‘The Regulator’, and airborne skank of ‘Thin Line’, and the harness-tugging pressure of ‘Dub Battle’, but they’re all held in check with a overarching slowness that gels the 12 tracks as a proper end-to-end listen in the manner of Pole’s early albums with a deeply reliable robustness and temper that stakes it out as arguably canonic tackle.

items.body:
Nueen follows production for Iceboy Violet and a string of releases for Quiet Time Tapes, Good Morning Tapes and Balmat, with a sprawling new album for 3XL, an ambient drill epic featuring guest spots from Dawuna, Space Afrika, Loraine James, Xzavier Stone and RenzNiro.

Everything clicked into place for Nacho Pezzati when he turned the humid soundscapes of his early releases into distorted beds for Iceboy Violet's casual free associations on the Hyperdub-released ‘You Said You'd Hold My Hand Through the Fire' back in 2024. He retains the same energy on 'Swerved', working alongside a team of vocalists and collaborators to locate a sweetspot between rap, dub and ambient vistas. His methodology is laid bare on 'Searchtiers', obscuring its UK drill-style sliding bass with weightless synths and gaseous FX, upping the ante when vocalist and producer Xzavier Stone jumps on the mic on 'Nowhere Near A Section'. The addition of proper hooks, adlibs and rhymes - "let it burn like Usher Raymond" - makes the production hit that much harder, not just referencing radio rap and R&B but challenging the paradigm. Fittingly, Loraine James, who early on inhabited similar zones, lends her voice to the grimy 'Atmosphere is my Style', whispering over Pezzati's hair metal samples and booming 808 Mafia-style basses. 

Manny's own RenzNiro checks in on 'Impls', rhyming over one of Nueen's most decisive beats, all clipped snares, gong samples and tweaked bass. And Space Afrika turn up with an assist on the low-slung highlight 'Shm', a smoove and sensual D'Angelo-style soul banger with none other than Dawuna on the mic. Dawuna returns on 'Matrix', splitting duties with Xzavier Stone who provides an impressive '00s post-jiggy hook and Pezzati's vision materialises. The haze of half-remembered bites of cloud rap, pop and club rap represents a post-P2P hauntology that's global, not really localised. And connecting with Space Africa again on the closing track 'I Guess', he travels beyond the boundaries of the album itself, lavishing SA's orchestral cries with fuzzy synths and swirling vocals.

items.body:
Mike Paradinas picks 18 scuzzy examples of Nondi_’s wistful take on footwork, ambient noise, and dub techno as an addendum to a strong eponymous 2nd album, nodding to precedents from Actress, AFX, µ-Ziq...

"Following her acclaimed 2023 release Flood City Trax, a dreamy, lo-fi take on footwork inspired by the crumbling rust-belt city she calls home, Nondi returns to Planet Mu with her second self-titled album, Nondi…

While Nondi… retains some of the hazy, nostalgic atmosphere of Flood City Trax, it pushes her sound in bold new directions. “I made this album to capture the sense of freedom I used to get from music when I was first discovering it all,” Nondi says. “It’s meant to be cute, fun, kinda weird and emotional — but most of all, it’s a presentation of some of the prettiest tracks I’ve made.” Though she hasn’t really experienced club culture where she lives, her impressionistic productions evoke the surreal, lingering sounds of a night out — the melodic haze that hums in your ears as you drift off to sleep. Lo-fi and melodic, yet fluid and free, her music carries a sense of flight and intuitive logic. Nondi’s influences range widely — Actress, Aphex Twin, footwork, and the stranger edges of dub techno are all felt, yet she hallucinates them through her own weathered, dreamlike lens. Her tracks often build from clashing loops that evolve and transform organically, or from familiar genre elements reshaped by her instinct for misty, heart-wrenching melody. Nondi… is a uniquely moving and exploratory album that expands her sonic world even further. Lo-fi yet luminous, playful yet profound."

items.body: Label: Shifting Paradigm Records, 2026 Personnel - Bryan Murray: tenor saxophone; Adam Linz: bass; Dan Monaghan: drums. Boasting a catchy sound and enjoying genuine freedom within the structure, saxophonist and composer Bryan Murray leads a supple chord-less jazz trio featuring bassist Adam Linz and longtime associate drummer Dan Monaghan. With friendship and collaboration at the center of Wolf , Murray—who also leads the peculiar avant-garde-meets-country band Bryan and the Haggards, is a member of Moppa Elliott’s Unspeakable Garbage, and has performed with David Byrne and St. Vincent outside the jazz sphere—explores his own music, radiating energy and abandon in a way that keeps listeners fully engaged. “ Bombs ” kicks off with hooky, motivic saxophone firepower over agile drums and sturdy bass, channeling David S. Ware and the reed language of Threadgill’s Air over the tight-knit rhythmic web spun by Linz and Monaghan. Post-bop and avant-garde walk hand in hand here, while “ Curtain ”, delivered with a sensitive balladic touch, brings forth Monaghan’s mallet work and shimmering cymbal washes. There’s pensive lyricism cutting through the open spaces, and Murray’s cautious melody is closely shadowed by Linz. Evoking childhood memories in West Virginia, “ Dirtslide ” displays an irreverent, hard-bop-inflected elegance over a full-throttle swing that is briefly suspended to accommodate the conversational interaction between Linz and Monaghan. Tactical bass mobility and crisp drumming dominate until Murray’s return, his playing abounding in ideas, supported by a firmly grounded and energetic rhythm section. The folksy theme of this piece contrasts with the pure modal jazz of “ Buell ”, a passionate prayer that recalls the spiritual hymns of John Coltrane and Billy Harper. “ Cloud Shapes ” is anchored by Linz’s impeccable bass guidance, while Monaghan’s cymbal work and mallets transport us to distant worlds. Murray’s narrative gift is unmistakable here. The title track, “ Wolf ”, achieves an air of mystery through a simple yet relentless bass ostinato. Deliberately measured, it unfolds in a lugubrious 3/4, while the closer, “ Fill Taker ”, embraces avant-garde elasticity, with Murray’s authoritative presence enhanced by well-delineated lines and motifs over a vibrant rhythmic foundation. This is stirring, serious sax-bass-drums work, resulting in a contemporary jazz album well worth digging into. Favorite Tracks: 01 - Bombs ► 03 - Dirtslide ► 05 - Buell ► 08 - Fill Taker

items.body:
LAUNCHPAD officially stepped into the spotlight on 3 August with its inaugural media event at PJ Performing Arts Centre in Kuala Lumpur, introducing a new artist growth platform designed to help emerging acts expand their reach across Southeast Asia.

Developed by Fast Track Entertainment in partnership with Sony Music Malaysia, LAUNCHPAD brings together intimate live showcases, regional media exposure, original digital content and brand partnerships to support artists as they grow beyond their home markets.

The official unveiling welcomed members of the media, industry partners and invited guests for the platform's first public introduction, while highlighting its vision of creating stronger connections between artists, audiences and the wider entertainment ecosystem across the region.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by GOKPOP (@gokpop_gallery)

The event featured appearances from KIIRAS, the six-member global K-pop girl group from South Korea; UPRIZE, Vietnam's rising seven-member boy group; and Malaysian entertainment icon Yusry Abdul Halim, who also participated in the programme alongside representatives from Fast Track Entertainment and Sony Music Malaysia. Live showcase performances and exclusive media interview sessions gave attendees an early look at the platform's artist-first approach.

Speaking during the launch, Fast Track Entertainment CEO Harris Lim shared that LAUNCHPAD represents an important milestone in the company's vision of building a more connected entertainment ecosystem across Southeast Asia. He said the platform was created around intimate live showcase experiences that connect artists directly with audiences, media, brands and industry partners, while creating new commercial opportunities that support long-term regional growth.

Unlike traditional artist development initiatives, LAUNCHPAD is designed to extend beyond the stage. Each showcase will be supported by regional media engagement, original digital content, industry networking and brand collaborations, helping artists strengthen their visibility and build sustainable careers across Southeast Asia.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by LAUNCHPAD (@launchpadexperience)

Following its official unveiling, LAUNCHPAD is set to roll out showcase editions across Southeast Asia from late 2026 through early 2027, with more participating artists, locations and programme details to be announced in the coming months.

AXEAN Festival 2026 will take over Jimbaran Hub in Bali, Indonesia, on 29–30 August, bringing together artists and music industry professionals from across Asia and beyond.

The lineup features D’MASIV, Ndarboy Genk, Arivu, Masdo, and Nerd Connection, alongside regional favourites Subsonic Eye, PLAYERTWO, Yellow Fang, Crystal Murray, ALYSON, and Basboi.

Spanning indie rock, alternative pop, hip-hop, soul, electronic jazz, progressive rock, dream pop, and contemporary Asian sounds, the bill will also include Aelea, Babon, Basajan, Bishnu Paneru, brkfstblend, Cactus Cactus, can't be Blue, Ciggarats, Clever Moose, Cupnoodle, Drizzly, El Karmoya, Emptyyy, Feral Stripes, GEE EXCLSV, GENIUS Flow, Given, hailinhtasm, INSPIRATIVE, Jo Soegono, Laze and Mardial, Lil Asian Thiccie x dj magn3sium, Littlefingers, Litty, LOR, Mayu, MRCH, Noni, Novocrane, Pitahati, Satu Per Empat, Scamper, Silly Silky, SLOWWVES, sub:shaman, Treaks, and YuuHai.

Gavendri and Olsam are also scheduled to deliver special performances at the festival’s invite-only opening party.

One of this edition’s biggest milestones is the Asian debut of Live on KEXP. The Seattle-based public radio station and music platform KEXP will record exclusive live sessions with selected artists during the festival.

The partnership aims to help independent artists from Southeast Asia reach wider international audiences by bringing KEXP’s recording team directly to the region.

AXEAN Festival will also host KOREA SPOTLIGHT, the K-music showcase presented by South Korea’s Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism and the Korea Creative Content Agency.

can't be Blue, MRCH, Nerd Connection, and Silly Silky will make their Indonesian debuts as part of the programme. All four artists emerged from MUSE ON, KOCCA’s artist discovery and development initiative, and will also appear at a dedicated KOREA SPOTLIGHT showcase in Jakarta.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by AXEAN Festival (@axeanfestival)

This year will also see the introduction of SEA URBAN, a programme dedicated to Southeast Asia’s hip-hop, rap, R&B, and contemporary urban music scenes.

The programme will combine a curated artist showcase with an industry panel examining the region’s evolving identities, rapid growth, and increasing global reach.

Festivalgoers can also expect an expanded songwriting camp and a Southeast Asian hawker-inspired food experience, adding more opportunities for collaboration and cultural exchange beyond the performances.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by AXEAN Festival (@axeanfestival)

Launched in 2020, AXEAN Festival has featured 200 artists from 20 countries across its first six editions. It has also welcomed 420 delegates from 32 countries and drawn close to 18,000 attendees to its in-person events.

Tickets to AXEAN Festival 2026 are now available via www.loket.com/o/axeanfestival.

items.body:
For generations of Singaporeans, National Day songs have served as more than ceremonial singalongs. They've become part of the country's collective memory, tied to school assemblies, National Day Parade celebrations, and moments of shared pride. With Celebrating Singapore: Volume 3, Music & Drama Company (MDC) isn't looking to replace those memories—it is inviting listeners to hear them through a fresh lens.

Released as the third instalment in MDC's Celebrating Singapore series, the four-track tribute album takes familiar National Day Parade classics and reimagines them with contemporary pop production inspired by international artists such as Michael Jackson, Maroon 5, Zara Larsson, and Shila Amzah. The result is a collection that bridges nostalgia with modern musical sensibilities while introducing these songs to a younger audience.

Rather than opting for straightforward remakes, each track embraces a distinct sonic identity.

Opening the record, 'Reach Out For The Skies' swaps its stadium-ready energy for a groove rooted in the disco-funk spirit of Michael Jackson's Off The Wall. Performed by RINES alongside aküma, the reworked version retains the optimism of the original while adding a rhythm that feels equally suited to today's playlists.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Music & Drama Company (MDC) (@musicanddramacompany)

Elsewhere, aküma returns on 'Breathing City', where producer Weiwen Seah draws from the restrained emotional pull of Maroon 5's 'This Love'. The production strips things back with expressive piano and understated instrumentation, pushing the singer into unfamiliar territory and showcasing a different side of his genre-blending artistry.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Music & Drama Company (MDC) (@musicanddramacompany)

Dominic Chin steps into the spotlight with 'Shine On Me', a soaring reinterpretation inspired by the grandeur of Shila Amzah's celebrated 'Yang Cong' performance. The arrangement gradually builds towards a cinematic climax, transforming the National Day anthem into something that feels equally at home on a concert stage.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Music & Drama Company (MDC) (@musicanddramacompany)

Perhaps the album's biggest surprise arrives with Gail Belmonte's rendition of 'Home'. One of Singapore's most beloved songs is given an EDM makeover before erupting into a dubstep-infused chorus inspired by Zara Larsson's 'Midnight Sun'. It's an ambitious rework that demonstrates how even the country's most recognisable anthem can evolve without losing its emotional core.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Music & Drama Company (MDC) (@musicanddramacompany)

The project also highlights a cross-section of Singapore's contemporary music scene. Alongside established performers like Dominic Chin and Gail Belmonte, the album spotlights rising voices including aküma and RINES, whose individual musical identities bring new perspectives to songs many listeners already know by heart.

More than a nostalgia project, Celebrating Singapore: Volume 3 presents a conversation between generations. By pairing iconic National Day songs with modern production styles and homegrown talent, MDC demonstrates how familiar melodies can continue to resonate long after their original debut—reminding listeners that national anthems, much like music itself, can keep evolving with the people who sing them.

Celebrating Singapore: Volume 3 is available on all major listening platforms including Kakee, Spotify, Apple Music and YouTube. For more information on MDC, visit its social media platforms Facebook, Instagram and TikTok.

items.body:
Music knows no borders on this season of Singer 2026.

The hit Chinese competition series is flexing its most international lineup yet, bringing together award-winning veterans and emerging artists from around the world for a season that celebrates cross-cultural performances on Hunan TV and Mango TV.

Leading the lineup is Jessie J, who returns to the Singer stage after previously appearing on the franchise. The British singer showcased her powerhouse vocals with performances of 'My Way' and 'California', reminding audiences why she remains one of the show's standout international guests.

Joining her is John Legend, who made his Singer debut this season. The EGOT-winning artist delivered renditions of 'All of Me' and 'Imagine', pairing his signature piano accompaniment with soulful vocals in a performance that resonated with both the live audience and viewers watching online.

The season also shines a spotlight on a new generation of international talent.

American singer Stanaj introduced viewers to his original track 'Romantic', blending R&B and electronic influences in his debut appearance on the programme.

Representing Malaysia, Azora Chin has impressed audiences with his versatility across multiple genres. Throughout the competition, he has performed songs including 'March', 'As a Monster', and 'Grandma's Words', showcasing both his storytelling and vocal range.

Meanwhile, British singer Elliot James Reay made his China debut as a substitute contestant. His performance of 'Skyfall' helped him advance to the show's "King of Songs Sprint Month" stage, highlighting the series' growing platform for emerging global artists.

By pairing internationally recognised names with rising performers from across the world, Singer 2026 continues to expand its global reach while introducing audiences in China to diverse musical voices.

A new acoustic-first music festival is making its way to the Philippines. Harana Music Festival is set to debut on 28 November at Filinvest Event Grounds in Alabang, Muntinlupa City, bringing together some of OPM's biggest names for what organisers describe as a more intimate and stripped-back festival experience.

Leading the lineup is TJ Monterde, joined by Clara Benin, Maki, Arthur Nery, Toneejay, Earl Agustin, Angela Ken, Nicole, Syd Hartha, Rob Daniel, and A!KA. The inaugural edition will spotlight acoustic-driven performances, placing the focus on live musicianship, storytelling, and closer connections between artists and audiences.

Unlike large-scale festival productions, Harana Music Festival aims to offer a more laid-back atmosphere, with raw vocals and live instrumentation taking centre stage. The concept is designed to create a setting where every performance feels personal while showcasing some of the country's most beloved singer-songwriters and rising acts.

Tickets are now available from PHP 1,000, with organisers expecting strong demand ahead of the festival. Harana Music Festival is presented by Epic Events, the team behind Aurora Music Festival and Maison Matcha.

items.body:
National Day Parade 2026 is set to transform the National Stadium into one enormous stage on 9 August, bringing together 36 artistes and more than 2,600 performers for Singapore’s 61st birthday.

Returning to the venue for the first time in a decade, this year’s show is framed around the theme Majulah Singapura, Go Beyond!. Across its pre-parade programme and six chapters, audiences can expect everything from electro-pop and Karnatik music to vintage Singapore tunes, beloved television themes and stadium-sized singalongs.

Hosting the evening are Joakim Gomez, Hafidz Rahman, Udaya Soundari, Xixi Lim and Gurmit Singh. William Xavier, affectionately known as Mr X, returns as the “Voice of NDP”. He will be joined by first-time NDP announcer Joanna François.

The celebration also arrives with the first Go Beyond: NDP 2026 Album, which brings together original compositions and reimagined favourites. Spanning uplifting anthems, heartfelt ballads, contemporary pop and electronic music, its songs form part of the show’s journey through Singapore’s heritage, shared memories and hopes for the future.

Pre-Parade

Before the parade officially begins, the hosts will welcome audiences back to the National Stadium with a series of singalongs and warm-up activities.

The programme includes a rehearsal of ‘Giants’, written by weish and performed by Iman Fandi, followed by the ‘Singapore Town–Tapau’ medley. Audiences can also expect quizzes, an introduction to this year’s NDP Pack and a segment marking the 60th anniversary of the National Pledge.

As NDP goes live, the cinematic Flag Relay film will follow the National Flag through Singapore’s heartlands and familiar locations. The action will then move from screen to stadium as the flag enters the venue for a live relay.

Athletes and para-athletes from Team Singapore will carry the flag around the stage alongside student-athletes from the Singapore Sports School. The relay will feature prominent sporting figures including Paralympic swimmer Yip Pin Xiu, kitefoiler Max Maeder and indoor skydiver Kai Minejima-Lee.

Chapter One: Go Beyond Self

The Go Beyond Self chapter places the spotlight on the Parade and Ceremony, which will feature 32 contingents and the largest civilian parade participation in more than a decade.

The proceedings will begin with the entry of the Guard of Honour, Colours Party and Combined Band. The Guard of Honour comprises contingents from the Army, Navy, Air Force, Digital and Intelligence Service, Singapore Police Force and Singapore Civil Defence Force.

The Combined Band brings together musicians from the Singapore Armed Forces Central Band, Singapore Police Force Band, Singapore National Cadet Corps Command Band and National Police Cadet Corps Band.

Collectively, the parade’s contingents will represent all six pillars of Total Defence, reflecting the role that Singaporeans play in keeping the country strong.

Key ceremonial moments include the State Flag Flypast, Feu De Joie and the 21-Gun Presidential Gun Salute. For the first time, the salute will be fired afloat at Kallang Basin.

Chapter Two: Go Beyond the Ordinary

The Go Beyond the Ordinary chapter begins with the SAF Band carrying the show out of the ceremonial proceedings through a stirring musical transition. Its performance will be accompanied by a high-energy routine from Martial House.

At the centre of the chapter is the People’s Parade, a colourful procession celebrating everyday Singaporeans whose service, passion and dedication have made a difference to those around them.

Eighteen floats will move through the performance space, representing six foundational values: Protect, Provide, Create, Build, Care and Justice.

Following a humorous skit involving the hosts, the chapter will conclude with a musical face-off between Ric Liu and the Shiok Sistas. The two sides will trade local tunes in a friendly competition, with spectators invited to join in using their voices and thundersticks.

Also appearing in the chapter are Jackie Pereira, Jalyn Han, Alin Mosbit and Annetha Ayyavoo.

The production will feature performers from Unity Secondary School, Beatty Secondary , Edgefield Secondary School, Tampines Meridian Junior College and St Andrew’s Junior College.

Chapter Three: Go Beyond Our Size

The Go Beyond Our Size chapter shifts from the high-energy mood of the People’s Parade into a more reflective exploration of Singapore’s maritime heritage, cultural roots and connections with the world.

It begins with a cinematic film about the nation’s relationship with the sea, followed by Asnida Daud performing ‘Aok Diko’, meaning “Yes, Of Course”. Sung in the Orang Laut dialect, the piece explores coastal identity, belonging and Singapore’s connection to its waters.

Asnida will be accompanied by a multi-ethnic group of drummers and 700 performers from Soka Gakkai Singapore. Larger-than-life puppets depicting native animals, including the tapir and mousedeer, will bring local folklore and biodiversity into the stadium.

Sushma Soma will follow with a Karnatik ode to Singapore. Marine-animal puppets and trading ships will move through the performance space, transforming the stadium floor into an underwater and seafaring spectacle.

Electronic duo NADA will then bring Singapore’s musical past into conversation with the present, fusing nostalgic local sounds with contemporary electronic beats. The act will be represented by Safuan Johari.

For the chapter’s finale, Asnida, Sushma and NADA will unite for ‘Song for Singapore’. The multi-ethnic drummers will return to join the artistes and Soka Gakkai performers for the musical conclusion.

Rizman Putra is also part of the chapter’s artiste lineup. Its performing partners include Damaru Singapore, the Eurasian Drum Ensemble, Nadi Singapura and ZingO Festival Drum Group.

Chapter Four: Go Beyond Time

The Go Beyond Time chapter turns the National Stadium into a television time machine, revisiting the programmes, songs, personalities and campaigns that have shaped Singapore’s popular culture.

The chapter begins with a short film depicting the five hosts as children in a 1960s kampong, encountering television for the first time.

Joakim Gomez will then perform an excerpt from ‘A World of Tomorrows’, followed by Hafidz Rahman dancing to the opening theme from Mat Yoyo.

Gurmit Singh will step back into the unmistakable yellow boots of Phua Chu Kang, while Xixi Lim will perform ‘Moonlight in the City’, or ‘城里的月光’. Udaya Soundari will close the main sequence with the theme from the Vasantham police drama Vettai.

Najip Ali will add another blast from the past with ‘Ren-tak Oonik’.

More than 300 performers from the People’s Association will bring the chapter to life alongside the Music and Drama Company, Singapore Airlines staff and mascots inspired by memorable national campaigns.

Together, the performances form a playful channel-surf through the television memories and cultural touchpoints that have connected generations of Singaporeans.

Chapter Five: Go Beyond Our Limits

The Go Beyond Our Limits chapter launches NDP into the future with electronic music, aerial choreography and the parade’s first indoor drone light show.

It opens with a kinetic typography film featuring words associated with Singapore’s culture. The chapter then shifts into high gear as Jasmine Sokko descends onto the stage alongside two aerialists while performing ‘You’ll Be Okay’.

Three hundred drones will move in synchrony with the performers 30 metres above the ground, combining music, technology and movement in one of the evening’s biggest visual spectacles.

The electronic momentum will continue with Han Oh and ‘Zero G-Roll’. Seven dancers will rise through stage lifts for a tightly synchronised routine matching the track’s electronic pulse.

Ranging from eight to 29 years old, the group includes an autistic dancer and a dancer with Down syndrome. The performers also represent Singapore’s four major ethnic groups.

Singer-songwriter Sky Shen will bring the chapter to a close with ‘March On With Me’, accompanied by six vocalists from the Music and Drama Company and dancers from Ministry of Education schools.

The performance will provide a reflective transition into the final chapter of the show.

Chapter Six: Go Beyond, Together

The concluding Go Beyond, Together chapter brings the evening’s music, sporting spirit and message of collective progress together.

It begins with Roar!, a short documentary centred on the stories of four sports coaches and the perseverance of Singapore’s sporting community.

The film will lead into Iman Fandi’s performance of ‘Giants’ alongside the 61-member The People’s Choir. Sixty-one coaches and athletes will also take the stage, connecting the song’s message of lifting one another up with the determination of Singapore’s sporting community.

The mood will then shift from reflective to celebratory as Gareth Fernandez, Dru Chen and The People’s Choir perform ‘Sparkle’, an upbeat singalong centred on individuality, confidence and togetherness.

Irene Jansen will also appear as part of the finale chapter’s artiste lineup.

The show will then move into the Majulah Moment, when Singaporeans will be invited to recite the National Pledge and sing the National Anthem.

Finally, DJ LENERD will lead a stadium-wide singalong featuring rearranged National Day songs, bringing the evening to an exuberant close.

Across its six chapters, NDP 2026 presents Singapore not through one definitive musical style, but through a chorus of traditions, generations and communities.

From Asnida Daud’s exploration of Orang Laut identity and Sushma Soma’s Karnatik performance to Jasmine Sokko’s aerial electro-pop spectacle and Iman Fandi’s stadium-sized rendition of ‘Giants’, this year’s show is shaping up to be both a celebration of how far Singapore has come and an invitation to imagine where it might go next.

items.body:
kiOra took their first step onto the international stage with an opening performance at CENTRAL MUSIC & ENTERTAINMENT FESTIVAL in Kuala Lumpur on 1 August.

Performing at Zepp Kuala Lumpur, the four-member Japanese girl group appeared before a Malaysian audience for their first-ever show outside Japan. The set marked a major milestone for kiOra as they introduced their music and self-described “Tokyo Hyper City Pop” sound to fans overseas.

The group performed their debut single, 'Coco', with the crowd’s cheers leaving a strong impression on the members.

“Getting to perform kiOra’s first song 'Coco' and sing it together with everyone was amazing! Jom jumpa lagi!” OTO shared after the show.

KYLA added, “Thank you to everyone who came today! It was the best. The 'Coco' MV is coming out soon, so please get ready to watch and rewatch! Can’t wait to meet again.”

RUKA also reflected on the audience’s response, saying, “I was so happy to hear your cheers during our first overseas performance. I hope we can sing 'Coco' together again!”

YU shared, “I was energized by today’s CENTRAL performance. I’ll keep doing my best to share our first single 'Coco' with even more people around the world!”

The Kuala Lumpur appearance followed kiOra’s unveiling at HEAD IN THE CLOUDS Tokyo, where the group first introduced its blend of hyperpop and city pop influences.

During their CENTRAL appearance, kiOra also announced that the official music video for 'Coco' will premiere worldwide on 8 August, alongside the single’s digital release.

'Coco' draws its title from the phrase “in my core” and the Japanese words “ima coco”, meaning “here and now”. The track centres on embracing one’s present self and finding the courage to move forward before feeling fully ready.

The single was created with producers and songwriters her0ism, Yaeji, Mechatok and Kanata Okajima, with Chelsea Warner joining the songwriting team. Recording took place at StudioBeat3, while vocal production was handled by Ashley Alish.

items.body:
CORTIS turned their Lollapalooza debut on 1 August  into one of the festival's standout moments, delivering an adrenaline-fuelled set that showcased exactly why the rookie quintet has been building momentum over the past year.

Despite persistent rain and delayed festival gates, fans flooded the T-Mobile Stage as soon as entry opened, filling the grounds ahead of the group's afternoon performance. By the time MARTIN, JAMES, JUHOON, SEONGHYEON, and KEONHO took the stage, chants of the group's name had already taken over the crowd.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Lollapalooza (@lollapalooza)

Opening with their breakout single 'GO!', CORTIS wasted no time establishing the pace. Backed by a live DJ, the five-piece powered through fan favourites including 'What You Want', 'REDRED', and 'ACAI', pairing razor-sharp choreography with commanding live vocals that rarely let the energy dip. Even festivalgoers unfamiliar with the group found themselves swept up in the performance, with singalongs growing louder as the set progressed.

The biggest surprise arrived midway through the show when hip-hop veteran Juicy J emerged to perform 'MOTION (feat. Juicy J)' live for the very first time, just days after the collaboration's release. The performance highlighted the chemistry between the artists, with MARTIN introducing the rapper as a "big brother" before the two acts celebrated together on stage.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Jordan Houston (@juicyj)

The set briefly shifted gears with the smoother 'JoyRide' before ramping back up through 'Mention Me', 'YOUNGCREATORCREW', 'Wassup', and 'TNT'. Closing number 'FaSHioN' brought one final surge of energy, as thousands of fans danced and shouted along until the last beat.

The performance capped off a whirlwind weekend for the group, who had also packed out a sold-out headline show at Chicago's House of Blues the night before. Together, the two performances underscored CORTIS' growing reputation as a formidable live act capable of translating their high-octane sound from studio recordings to festival stages.

Speaking after the performance, the members reflected on achieving a longtime dream,"Performing at Lollapalooza Chicago has been a dream of ours since we were young, so being able to experience this moment was truly special. While working on GREENGREEN, we imagined the kind of energy we hoped to create on stage, and seeing that vision come to life with fans made this experience even more meaningful."

Following their Lollapalooza debut, CORTIS are set to kick off the sold-out North American leg of their first headline tour on 4 August in Toronto. For more information, visit ibighit.com/ko/cortis/tour.

items.body:
Mark Tuan has released his latest single, 'Alone', his first offering of 2026.

Following the introspective themes of his Silhouette EP, the new track sees the GOT7 member and solo artist dive deeper into feelings of emotional isolation, overthinking, and the quiet moments that come with being alone. Built around atmospheric R&B production, layered harmonies, and expressive melodies, 'Alone' also marks a notable evolution in Mark's sound.

The single was co-written by singer-songwriter Tone Stith, while production comes from Peyote, whose recent credits include Doechii's Alligator Bites Never Heal. Together, they help shape a track that balances vulnerability with sonic experimentation, reflecting Mark's desire to push beyond his creative comfort zone.

Speaking through the song's emotional landscape, Mark explores the tension between escapism and loneliness, capturing the restless thoughts that surface during late-night drives and moments of solitude. Rather than hiding those emotions, he leans into them, offering listeners one of his most personal releases to date.

items.body: Run by our very own Joseph Sannicandro, the Lost Children Net Label has been quiet as a Bandcamp imprint, but kept alive through Joseph’s podcasts and newsletter posts since the 2022 release of the massive 56-track [Useless Sounds]. Returning in full force with a triptych of tapes, Lost Children is ready to reclaim its place at the forefront of experimental music. The crown jewel of the bundle is CRACKS, a gathering of international musicians who address the “concept of the border as a colonial wound.” Proceeds benefit the Council on American-Islamic Relations Minnesota and Lumpen Radio (an initiative of the Public Media Institute in Chicago). The confrontational words on the cover have become a global rallying cry. Joni Void starts the set off with “Borders,” cutting right to the chase. The percussion sounds like a jailer’s baton dragged across prison bars. A connection is made between physical borders, sonic borders and the borders of perception, with dialogue interrupted by the siren and blare of a local enforcement agent. Martín Rodríguez shares radio transmissions heard from the Arizona-Mexico border where he was raised, giving credit to radio for helping him to recover from a brain tumor. The transmissions sparkle and fade, as if underlining the name of the Lost Children imprint. One thinks of voices and souls lost and the search for missing loved ones, possibly deported, possibly dead. Kate Carr offers bucolic bells bisected by the essential chaos of street protests, suggesting that the comfortable must be disturbed in order for substantive change to unfold. Lubo Alexandrov‘s bucolic “Echoes (from the other side)” doesn’t identify which side it refers to, leaving the interpretation wide open. Speaker Music‘s haunting, echoed, abraded and ultimately percussive “Moral Injury” exposes the deepest rupture of the crisis as an affront to goodness itself. Sannicandro’s own “rethink not reform” brings the sound to the streets, the appealing “Wait” of an electronic crossing signal contrasted with a sense that the fragile peace is about to be disturbed; in layers of increasing ferocity, it is. The disorientation of the intimate soundscape imitates that of the assaulted. apartment52‘s “i would die for anything, maybe” exposes a different insecurity while repeating the effect of messages that fail to get through. A heartfelt live recording from Hamza Lahmadi connects the yearning of sojourners around the world, who just want a place to call home. Mai Mai Mai incorporates waves as siren call, implying both the hope of welcome and the lack of permission to land. The drone is lonely and isolated, the land right there. Anas Hajam lightens the mood a bit with finger-picking goodness and breath; one needs encouragement such as this. Then Joni Void returns as the remixer of Soledad Rosas‘ “Piel,” which extends the references to breath along with vocal glissandos and tender song. The intake just prior to the second minute recalls George Floyd. Only a minute long, Esther B.‘s “molti sport” is a rush of static awaiting definition. Then comes a reference to Greek mythology: thenewobjective feat. Cole Pulice use “Scylla and Charybdis” to reference the idiom “the lesser of two evils,” summarizing the current state of border disputes, in which no one wins. Stefan Christoff closes the compilation with “Turn,” whose tolling church bells, echoed on prepared piano, are both indictment and call to arms. Two artists featured on CRACKS also branch out across the bundle. ATMOSPHERICS is taken from a series of soundscape broadcasts prepared by Diana Duta & Stefan Christoff. Partially recorded on the silver anniversary of Portugal’s Carnation Revolution, “Paysage sonare” is a tribute to victory, a long battle finally won. The sounds of the coast are sounds of peace in both senses of the word. Soft ambient tones unify the composition, wresting control from the field recordings in the tenth minute before ceding space in the eighteenth and again in the thirty-first, ending in familial laughter and joy. Similar sounds launch the title track, recorded in Brussels. The piece eventually branches into the northern marshes, calling on hydrophones for a glance below the surface. The contrast between city and marsh recalls CRACKS: the discussion of desirable environments, “migration, political dissent and resistance.” The link becomes overt in the chants of the twenty-first minute. Again Christoff’s synth, along with pensive guitar, is the glue that holds the work together, although even this is lost in time, rescued from older tapes, a subtle metaphor. In the long aquatic segment that closes the piece, one feels retreat and resolution. Esther B. is also Esther Bourdages, whose cassette Listening session, live concerts, figure skating “turns the turntable into a destructive instrument.” These live improvisations expose the turntable as preserver and destroyer of memory. Segments rise through the ether intact, only to be savaged with love. There’s a huge difference between turntablism in a hip-hop sense and turntablism in an experimental sense, but the two are not exclusive. In her preference for the older, even archival records, Bourdages honors The Caretaker; in her disdain for the creation of linear narratives or danceable samples, she honors Kid Koala. “figure skating” flips the script, conflating the stylus and the skate, the vinyl and the ice, with few if any identifiable markers until the end: a mesmerizing lesson in abstraction and a companion to Curling. In “Earache, My Eye,” a horrified son protests to his father, “You ruined my record, man!” Such a thing does not exist in Bourdages’ world, where records are purposely altered by “grinding, cutting and sanding.” If anything, the imperfections are the draw. Yet it is obvious that the artist loves her collection, teasing sounds from these records that were never intended to be heard, like coaxing stories from a childhood friend. It is passing strange to hear them on a cassette, although in the hands of another this might be manipulated in a different way, then passed to a digital specialist for further dismantling. We once thought that sound, once recorded, was fixed; we believe so no longer. Welcome back, Lost Children! (Richard Allen)

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Gianni Leone has remained active since the era of YS, the album for which he is best remembered, and it was in this spirit that Il Balletto di Bronzo returned to craft a highly distinctive work. Rich in nuance and imagery, it evokes a dark, ominous, and theatrical atmosphere; performing as a trio, the band ingeniously constructs a soundscape that suggests specific moods and settings, scenes suspended in time and space where the very concepts of time and space begin to lose their meaning."Oceani Sconosciuti" carries an air of silent-film horror reminiscent of the band Crucis, while the atonal counterpoint found throughout the album also shares common ground with the music of Van Der Graaf Generator. Gianni handles the vocals, lending Lemures a distinct avant-garde aura."L'Emofago" features a powerful drum foundation reminiscent of Led Zeppelin; the atmosphere created by the keyboards and the lyrics of this concept �lbum, which incorporates symphonic Minimoog flourishes and operatic recitatives within a hard rock (bordering on heavy metal) context, complements Gianni's soaring vocals. It evokes lightning bolts and tremors raining down upon Sodom and Gomorrah, all delivered by the trio in this magnificent progressive work. It suggests that the best of the 70s never truly faded away; rather, updated for the present, that spirit remains more vital than ever, especially since the music avoids sounding merely "vintage."Napoli Sotterranea paints vivid mental images, an entire movie, really. Keyboards take on the role of guitars, while the vocals explore mystical Eastern melodies, accompanied by a drum and bass foundation that occasionally borders on psychedelia before embracing jazz-rock, though of a violent, provocative, and aggressive variety. This is not the comeback of an established band merely recreating the past; rather, it is a group intent on offering something new and making a fresh contribution to the musical landscape.There is melody in L'Ombra Degli Dei... ideas are laid out; it is music that is alive, in the tradition of Italian progressive rock, drawing upon its influences to forge something new. Following a keyboard introduction, an instrumental section transports us into a different world; each step of the staircase leads to a distinct realm. "Labyrinthus" blends Eddie Jobson's U.K.-style keyboards with Gianni Leone's operatic vocals, while a jazz section with a Canterbury-esque spirit permeates the entire piece; the trio delivers an impeccable performance, featuring an improvised section where time constraints seem irrelevant, that evokes a chamber-music atmosphere, ultimately allowing that blend of tragic and futuristic romanticism to return and take hold.The intricate, agile keyboard arrangements of "Certezze Fragili" contrast with the dense, suspended atmosphere of "Deliquio Viola," where this progressive-opera fusion is pushed to its absolute limits, akin to reconstructing a Renaissance past using parts from dismantled cars. They achieve the seemingly impossible; all that remains is to follow the rhythm as the keyboards and drums, pulsing with energy, lead us to "Il Vento Poi." There, echoes of the wind sweep the voices away, distorting them and blurring the lines between reality and time, exposing their relativity, and, by extension, their malleability, as well as the possibility of altering them through perception.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — The man who would fall to Earth in 1976 never truly stayed in one place; London, Detroit, Los Angeles, and Berlin always hosted him merely as a temporary traveler, a restless tenant destined to leave sooner or later. It was in this context that, after bidding farewell to Ziggy Stardust, he moved forward with that same band, featuring Mick Ronson, Trevor Bolder, and Mick Woodmansey, but also Ken Fordham on sax, three backing vocalists, and Mike Garson on piano, whose contribution would make all the difference.Naturally, lessons with Lindsay Kemp, the British dancer, actor, mime, choreographer, and set designer, helped shape the persona of Aladdin Sane, a character that offered a critique of the entertainment world and was inspired by the very tour during which the songs comprising the album were written.That same dichotomy, between the lightning bolt across his face and his stance regarding his newfound stardom, ultimately extended to the music itself; one can distinguish between Rolling Stones-esque blues-soul rockers like "Watch That Man," "Panic in Detroit," "Cracked Actor," a fast-paced glam version of "Let's Spend the Night Together," and "The Jean Genie," and other, more experimental tracks. The latter reveal the jazz-inflected and at times atonal influence of Mike Garson, as well as a cabaret DNA and darker, more evocative, compositionally complex themes, songs like "Aladdin Sane (1913-1938-197?)," "Time" (heavily influenced by Jacques Brel, an essential reference for understanding one of his earthly personas), "The Prettiest" (evoking the 1950s, a style that kept coming and going), and "Lady Grinning," a gem featuring a flamenco-style introduction. Both Mick Ronson on guitar and Mike Garson on piano earned their pivotal roles in creating that special magic, an artistic expression that would eventually lead him to portray Paul Ambrosius von Przygodski in the 1978 film Just a Gigolo: a young Prussian character drifting between two worlds yet finding a true home in neither, never fully belonging, much like Aladdin Sane.

items.body: Review by WaldoJeffers — As someone who really enjoys Conrad Schnitzler's early work with Kluster, Tangerine Dream and also solo, I consider "Gold" to be a highly convincing album, standing in the tradition of "Blau" and certainly "Rot", dating from the same creative period as this belatedly released album.Schnitzler experiments here once again with all sorts of electronically generated instruments; briefly, I even hear an accordion. You will search in vain for rhythms and harmonies here, of course; "Gold" is an album of free form. It chirps, pings and creaks merrily away; only in track 12 (the tracks have no titles) does something almost akin to a dance mood arise as a result of the electronic percussion; although even to this you can hardly dance, there is simply too much going on. An oriental-sounding flute improvises over heavy chirping and bubbling above the quasi-soloing percussion. Space techno? With the following track, "13", which sounds like a cool, empty factory hall turned into music, a bit of Industrial also comes into play."Gold" is fun and enormously entertaining for those people who (like me) find many of the productions of the "Berlin School" incredibly boring. Not a typical Conrad Schnitzler album, but for me (perhaps for that very reason) one of the best.

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — ProjeKct Three's 'Masque' comes straight from the R&D department of King Crimson. This is the thirdinstallment in the live project series featuring members of the 'THRAK' lineup of the Robert Fripp-led band, brought together with the aim of exploring off-beat ideas through improvisation andexperimentation. These are live recordings featuring alternating lineups of the 90s Crimson, withthis particular 1999 recording featuring the trio of Robert Fripp, Trey Gunn, and Pat Mastelotto. Asis the case with the majority of the KC releases from that period, the music played by ProjeKctThree incorporates the spacey ambient soundscapes patented by Fripp, together with the finely tunedWarr guitar of Trey Gunn and the impressive array of electronic percussion and loops played by PatMastelotto. The type of experimental rock presented on 'Masque', however, is more abstract and lessgroovy than the output of other ProjeKcts (like One or Two, which makes it closer to something like'Thrakattak' than the album 'THRAK' itself.The thirteen tracks making up this live album are numbered and (perhaps suggestively) left untitled,while the somewhat intimidating, surreal and impersonal cover art uncannily reflects the kind ofmusic played on 'Masque'. This is one of these experimental recordings that only make sense whenheard in their entirety, but if I were to outline several pieces of greater significance, I wouldhave to start with '1', which is an obnoxious and impulsive opener, replete with hefty bass tonesand obscure guitar licks. 'Masque 2' then presents a more sustained rock sound tinted with gentleambient soundscapes, while the complex rhythms on '3' weave around the haunting electronics in arather menacing way. Later on, 'Masque 7' represents another abstract-sided piece, impressing with asoft but prominent bass sound, whereas the industrial hue encompassing 'Masque 8' makes it one ofthe darker compositions heard on this album. It is also worth noting how effective the hypnoticallyabrasive sounds on '9' are, with the two final pieces also being among the highlights.Of all the ProjeKcts, Three might be the single most intriguing variation of Crimson - 'Masque' isunorthodox and compelling, but for me this is the kind of experimentation that drives the genreforward.

items.body: Review by AWizardATrueAimee — I've got quite the history with this album since my husband, who introduced me to progressive rock, had an email referring to it. That was back in 2009 and I've listened to it countless times since. I was so excited to see the band was releasing a remaster and I certainly have not been disappointed by it. Steve Wilson did such a great job on their other releases. I'll admit I was heartbroken but understanding that this album could present some difficulties. There's been some concerns about AI being used in this remaster that I somewhat understand but?. I don't think we'll be getting as clear and true of a version of this album otherwise. And if this is the way it's got to be done, I'm here for the ride. This remaster/remix showed me all sorts of instruments and sections that I didn't hear in the past which I'm really grateful for. An album which at times was previously impossible to parse is now much punchy and emotionally charged than ever. And the album title track has always rang to me as a Gentle Giant staple within their catalogue. It doesn't get much more progressive than this.

items.body: Impressed by this partnership’s Dvořák Ninth (review), I was eager to hear their Bruckner fourth, surely the composer’s most popular symphony both in the concert hall and on record. This new reading, while impressive, is not a complete success. Symphony No. 4 Amazon Presto Apple This reading lacks the instrumental weight and depth of color that I would argue makes for an authentic Bruckner sound. Having grown up listening to many Telarc recordings of this orchestra, I lay the blame for this deficiency on the engineering. The mics are placed too close to the musicians, surely to minimize audience noise during this live recording. There is little bloom to the sound, and no real hall ambience. Climaxes feel contained, and softer dynamics are limited by the proximity of the mics. Bruckner’s music was written with a warm, reverberant acoustic in mind, and that acoustic is an integral part of the sound. Not so here. Instead, it is like standing one foot away from Seurat’s A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte: every brush stroke is visible, and we might appreciate how the painting is assembled, but it comes at the cost of the image’s beauty, mystery and expression. The second issue has to do with the edition. There are now ten different editions of the fourth symphony to choose from. Stutzmann uses the late Benjamin-Gunnar Cohrs’ 2021 critical edition of the 1878–81 version, which has been recorded only once before, by Simon Rattle with the LSO (LSO Live). For that album Cohrs described his edition as “the second version of the ‘Romantic’ Symphony as it stood by the end of 1881,” including “Bruckner’s own suggested cut in the Finale.” But Stutzmann does not take the cut — why not? Why embrace a little-known version and then ignore one of its most significant, composer-sanctioned changes? The liner notes offer no discussion of the edition, nor is it listed on either side of the booklet cover. As to the performance itself, I had initially intended to limit comparisons to other American recordings, but it now seems best to set Stutzmann against Rattle (details – review). His performance is faster, with an overall timing of 61’30” against Stutzmann’s 71’39”, and the largest difference comes in the final movement, where Stutzmann restores the passage Bruckner marked for cutting. Each conductor belongs to a different interpretive school. Rattle recalls Karajan: a subtle use of rubato, polished orchestral sound with resplendent brass and gossamer strings, a unified pulse that keeps the structure in view. Stutzmann is far closer to Jochum: much freer rubato, a more heterogeneous orchestral sound and, more distinctively, an intensely songful rendering of Bruckner’s score. Nathalie Stutzmann conducts the Atlanta Symphony Orchestra. Photo © Rand Lines. Stutzmann’s approach is compelling in the second movement, though at 17’05” it feels more Adagio than Bruckner’s Andante quasi Allegretto. In the finale the flexibility sometimes compromises a sense of the overarching structure, and there are moments when the energy level dips precipitously low. This is less of an issue in the opening movement, where one does get to hear much of the contrapuntal inner voices. Both Rattle and Stutzmann solicit rounded articulation, and I often missed the cut and thrust of Blomstedt’s San Francisco account on Decca and Honeck’s Pittsburgh performance on Reference, especially in the Scherzo. Both drive the music harder, encouraging more wildness in the trumpet-capped climaxes. Bruckner described the Trio as “how a barrel-organ plays during the midday meal in the forest.” Honeck is perhaps best at capturing this rustic picture, even if he is reticent to allow an earthier, less refined sound. Stutzmann conjures a poised, lightly sprung elegance that I enjoyed, even though it hardly captures the composer’s description. In short, I find Stutzmann’s performance the more compelling of the two. Yet if I want to hear this edition, surely I want Bruckner’s cut in the finale. Rattle’s release adds to the symphony itself the discarded 1874/76 Scherzo and the 1878 Volksfest Finale, an extended early version of the Andante, and the unabridged 1881 Finale, a valuable addition for Bruckner specialists. Ultimately, neither recording compels me to embrace this version over the more familiar Haas and Nowak editions, and neither matches the brilliance of Blomstedt, Honeck, or the classic Böhm/Vienna/Decca. items.body: Mitsuko Uchida’s 2025 live performance of the late Beethoven sonatas (Op. 109–111) arrives almost two decades after her studio recording for Decca, and it carries the added weight of being her final account of these works. Her choice of Suntory Hall marks a homecoming: she has played there since the hall’s opening season in 1986, and remains its only Associate Artist. Last Three Sonatas Amazon Presto Apple The gap between the two readings naturally raises the question of how much her interpretations have developed. If we go by Op. 109, things have indeed changed: not a drastic pivot, but an amplification of certain aspects. The 2006 reading already had an appreciable fluidity, but in the newer Vivace (track 1) Uchida makes more unabashed pauses and rubatos that still fit naturally into the music. Some of the urgency of the earlier second movement has turned into greater dramatic power here, and the attention to articulation and secondary voices is never sacrificed. The temperament of the final movement (track 3) can vary considerably depending on the tempo of the opening theme. Where Serkin and Gilels move more slowly and evoke contemplation, Uchida is brisker than either of them, and her pace captures the cantabile of Beethoven’s marking. In the variations that follow, a deep familiarity reveals itself in her ability to balance forward motion against the emphasis the grandest moments need. Op. 110 comes alive through contrast. Uchida uses Beethoven’s textures to shift between lyricism and resonance. The arpeggios at the start of the Moderato cantabile (track 4), leading up to the second theme, are a prime example: they begin as shimmering filigree and morph into a resplendent presence — perhaps a fitting representation of the vocal and orchestral sides she brings out throughout. The Scherzo carries a much higher degree of austerity and insistence than the 2006 Decca version, though both readings remain entirely valid. The Adagio (track 6) reveals a performer who understands the profundity of late Beethoven: the desperation, the melancholy with its sharp poignancy, the gravitas of internal conflict and weariness. What is most captivating is her ability to convey the rawness of these sentiments in a live setting. Uchida’s Fuga (track 7) proves more multidimensional than many. The switch from minor to major is subtle, and it gives her room to explore the quieter sides of the fugue before it spins into something much larger. Even in the softest playing nothing sounds hurried. Pauses are placed to maximize dynamic contrast while delineating the intricacies of Beethoven’s structure. Mitsuko Uchida. Photo © Justin Pumfrey / Decca. Although it moves slightly slower at times than her previous interpretation, the new Op. 111 (tracks 8–9) embodies the severity and boldness of the Maestoso marking. The urgency of the prior account has developed into an equally compelling adamance. The calmness of the Arietta feels like an arrival after a long journey. The same weighty substance carries into the variations, which works for the most part, though the syncopated variation at 6’40” could take a touch more rhythmic vitality. What emerges most strongly, though, is the intricacy of the tender moments, which linger in their transcendence. The engineers have kept audience noise to a minimum, and the piano is captured with enough clarity to register its tone and regulation. As a final account of these sonatas this is a distinguished one, and the culmination of Uchida’s long engagement with them. items.body: Saint-Saëns completed his Symphony No. 3 in 1886, commissioned by the Philharmonic Society of London, and conducted the premiere himself at the age of fifty. It was the last symphony he would write, and it came at the height of his career. He is said to have remarked that he would never achieve anything like it again. When Franz Liszt died later that year, Saint-Saëns dedicated the score to his memory. The “Organ” nickname is a little misleading. The composer wrote not a concerto but a symphony “with organ,” where the instrument works inside the orchestra rather than in front of it. The scoring also calls for a piano, played at times by two players. The four traditional movements are folded into two continuous parts, unified by a single theme that keeps returning in new forms, a technique absorbed from Liszt. The music travels from restless C minor to a blazing C major finale, whose massive organ entrance has tested engineers as much as conductors. Recordings have answered that challenge in different ways, from concert-hall organs captured in place to a cathedral instrument recorded separately and mixed in. Here are The Classic Review editorial team’s recommendations for the best recordings of Saint-Saëns’s Symphony No. 3 (“Organ”). Boston Symphony Orchestra, Charles Munch More than sixty years after it was made, Charles Munch’s 1959 recording in Boston remains the one to beat. The thrill comes from playing of scorching intensity that unfolds like a live concert. Munch sets a fast tempo for the first movement’s main theme, and the rhythmic drive never lets up. The strings sing the *Poco adagio* with unforced lyricism, a reminder that this performance is not all fire. In the finale, Berj Zamkochian’s organ makes a thunderous entrance, its bass seeming to shake the floor. The aging tape strains audibly under that huge chord, yet the drama sweeps this flaw aside. Add Munch’s Debussy *La Mer* and Ibert *Escales* as couplings, and the disc’s legendary status is easy to understand. Munch Amazon Presto Apple Chicago Symphony Orchestra, Daniel Barenboim The organ heard on Daniel Barenboim’s 1976 Chicago recording was played an ocean away from the orchestra. Gaston Litaize recorded his part on the organ of Chartres Cathedral, and the two performances were joined afterward in the studio. That procedure could easily have sounded artificial, but the combined result has an epic, almost otherworldly presence. It crowns a performance of irresistible panache, with the Chicago brass playing at full strength and a finale of colossal impact. Barenboim’s invigorating first-movement tempo leaves the strings a little untidy in places, a small price for the sweep he achieves. It matches Munch for voltage while sounding far more modern. For the symphony’s raw physical thrill, this is the version to reach for. Barenboim Amazon Presto Apple Detroit Symphony Orchestra, Paul Paray Paul Paray’s 1957 Detroit account moves with exceptional lightness. Its appeal is not weight or blaze, but transparency and grace. Paray trained this orchestra himself, and it shows in the supple phrasing and the way every strand stays audible. Tempos are bracingly fast, yet nothing feels rushed. The playing stays composed even at full speed. The organ part is in the hands of Marcel Dupré, one of the great virtuosos of the twentieth century. Made with just three microphones, the recording remains astonishingly fresh for its age, clearer than Munch’s. For listeners who want to hear the elegance inside this symphony, Paray is the essential alternative. Paray Amazon Presto Apple Montreal Symphony Orchestra, Charles Dutoit Few discs did more to show off the young CD format than Charles Dutoit’s 1982 Montreal recording. Its lasting virtues, though, are musical: elastic, beautifully controlled phrasing and orchestral playing of rare polish. Peter Hurford’s organ is cleanly focused and never distorts, even in the loudest pages. Every detail sits in natural proportion. The coupling is the Second Piano Concerto, with Pascal Rogé as soloist. Those who crave the sheer force of Munch or Barenboim may find Dutoit reserved. Anyone meeting the symphony for the first time could not ask for a better guide. Dutoit Amazon Presto Apple Kansas City Symphony, Michael Stern Glorious sound is the first thing anyone notices about Michael Stern’s 2013 recording with the Kansas City Symphony. It is not, however, the main reason to recommend the album. The performance underneath has genuine vitality, with crisp rhythms and the rich, full-bodied sonority this music thrives on. Jan Kraybill presides over a big Casavant concert organ, and the recording gives it impressive depth and space. The couplings are generous: the *Introduction and Rondo capriccioso* with violinist Noah Geller, and the lesser-known *La Muse et le Poète*. A performance this alive earns its place beside the classics. Stern Amazon Presto Apple Top image ©️ The Classic Review, AI generated The form can be filled in the actual website url.
